attributes.label: Trials and pilots on  the island
attributes.description: The trials, pilots and demonstrations that parties beside the farmers run on the island and for its farms, each showing what a measure or a crop does under the island's conditions. The Living Lab Schouwen-Duiveland started officially in January 2019 as a place for parties who want to innovate together, to speed up the island's move to self-sufficient water management (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 8); its project Samenwerken voor Zoet Water (2020–2022), carried out with Deltares, KWR, Acacia Water, Agrarisch Schouwen-Duiveland and the municipality (Living Lab Schouwen-Duiveland, n.d.-a), made quickscans for 13 farmers (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 9), and a later one, of Acacia Water, Deltares, Delphy, the trial farm Rusthoeve, three farms and the municipality, demonstrated and monitored new drainage on the island (Living Lab Schouwen-Duiveland, n.d.-b), laid at Kerkwerve and Dreischor (Living Lab Schouwen-Duiveland, 2023). For crops, Delphy, with ZLTO and Saeftinghe Zilt, researched saline cultivation in 2014–2018 (Delphy, 2023, p. 49), and the trial farm Rusthoeve, at Colijnsplaat on Noord-Beveland, has experimented with crops since 2014 and laid out irrigation trials after 2018 (pp. 9, 19, 20, 24). A Constant: no source read shows the farms' choices moving the trials, so whether the trials answer what farmers do or ask for is a question for the group model building session.

attributes.label: Perceived risk of  switching
attributes.description: How much a farmer expects to lose by moving a field to a new crop, before moving it: a failed yield, no buyer, a low price, too little water, carried by the farm. It drives the decision before a switch, where Margin given up on high-margin crops is the outcome after it; Farmers' knowledge of new crops is whether a farmer knows how, this who pays when it fails. On the island, larger business risks slow innovation (Delphy, 2023, p. 6), crops grow so costly that they may not fail (p. 13), and the cost of innovative solutions lies mainly with the farmer while they are not yet proven, so investing carries a risk (p. 50). In a survey of farmers in the south-west Netherlands (2013), a higher perceived cost of drought measures lowered their adaptation and trust in their own competence raised it, both parts of how farmers appraise their ability to cope (van Duinen et al., 2015a, pp. 1089, 1091). Whether it runs through others' successes and failures is a question for the group model building session. An Auxiliary: it follows what farmers know and the contracts on offer. No actor: a perception, not a decision.

attributes.label: Buyer contracts for  new crops
attributes.description: Hectares of new or alternative crops that buyers contract with the island's farmers before the season. A contract takes risk off the farmer as far as its terms go, measured for potatoes nationally: a fixed-price contract guarantees the price for the agreed quantity, a day-price or volume contract only the sale, provided the crop meets the agreed quality, the price risk staying with grower and buyer both (Janssens et al., 2020, pp. 11–12); the contracted part carries an offtake duty, while potatoes beyond a hectare contract's volume mostly go at the day price, with none unless agreed (p. 12); contracts let a farmer hedge against price swings (p. 14), and a grower who sells free bears a loss alone (p. 15). So a contract moves the price and the sales risk, not the yield risk. For the new crops, Dutch quinoa is grown under contract for one distributor, which buys a pre-agreed amount at a fixed price and manages supply according to demand (de Wit et al., 2022, pp. 266, 268), a supermarket buys its own-brand quinoa from 12 Dutch farmers under a three-year contract (DutchNews.nl, 2026), and for saline crops in Zeeland the market is hard, with little room for new growers (Delphy, 2023, p. 49). No source read shows a buyer contracting a new crop on the island. An Auxiliary: set season by season.

attributes.description: What the island's arable farms owe their banks: the loans still to be repaid, which new credit adds to and repayments pay off, the repayment being the periodic amount that pays a loan back within the agreed term (ABN AMRO, n.d.-a). attributes.label: Arable farmers on  Schouwen-Duiveland
attributes.interest: Enough fresh water when their crops need it, above all as they germinate, to lower their farms' risk or to raise production, as the farmers of one cluster studied put it. Many want to invest in measures that hold fresh water, once the technique, its costs, its risks and its gain in yield are known for the island's conditions; while supply from outside and measures on the island are both still debated, they hold back.
attributes.influence: Decide what the island's farmland grows and how each field is drained, irrigated and supplied with water: in 2025, 200 farms registered on the island grew arable crops on 9,094 ha, of the 13,752 ha of farmland of its 240 farms. A measure in the subsoil can serve several neighbouring farms, which collect and tap its water together; the study of the island's farms explored measures for clusters of one to three. As owners of farmland they decide whether the water board may charge them more for a water supply project: at least half must respond and two thirds of those be in favour. On a draft water level plan they can send views within six weeks and, if affected, appeal at the court for six weeks after the decision. Score 5: they decide the adaptation itself.
attributes.affected: Their farms depend wholly on rain and on the fresh groundwater under the dunes, the creek ridges and the thin rainwater lenses of the low polders: the island has no link to the main freshwater system, so in dry periods no water can be brought in and no ditches flushed, its shallow groundwater and ditches carry much salt, and the farms run short of water; drought in the growing season, subsidence and sea level rise make this worse, and the dry years 2018–2020 showed the farms vulnerable. Delphy's report on the island's freshwater demand (2023) finds farming on the island impossible without more fresh water; in 2026 a potato grower at Nieuwerkerk lost a fifth of his harvest to drought, had stopped growing onions for want of fresh water, and found ditch water at times nearly as salt as the Oosterschelde. Adapting is uncertain for them: the measures that store fresh water in the subsoil are not yet fitted to the island's conditions, their costs, risks and gain in yield not yet sufficiently known, so many farmers will not take the investment risk while these uncertainties last. Delphy's study of the island (2023) finds the cost of innovative solutions lying mainly with the farmer while they are not yet proven, so investing carries a risk, and the farms with little room to invest; no relation on the map shares that risk with them.

attributes.label: Waterschap  Scheldestromen
attributes.interest: Safe dikes and dunes first; then an optimal use of the water system, its ditch levels matched to soil and land use, fresh water kept available where it can and fresh groundwater kept in stock, within costs society accepts. It has no task as a supplier of fresh water: measures beyond its regular water management are for the users of the fresh water to pay.
attributes.influence: Sets the island's ditch levels in its water level plans (peilbesluiten: Duiveland 2021, Schouwen 2022), for the waters the province designates, to be held as far as possible, matched as far as it can to soil type and land use such as farming, after a process with the people of the area; sets and enforces the rules for farms' groundwater extraction for irrigation in its waterschapsverordening, a notification within limits per hectare and per well, a permit beyond them. Its general board sets the levy that pays for its water management: for 2026 the owners of unbuilt land other than nature, farmland among them, carry 22.78% of the costs, at €115.53 a hectare, its base rate, with a higher one for paved public roads. It may charge the farmland a water supply project serves up to 100% more, once a stakeholder has asked for the project, at least half of the owners have responded and two thirds of those are in favour; it charges more for its supply projects on Tholen and Sint Philipsland (10 to 50%) and in the Reigersbergsche polder (35 to 45%). It can take project decisions and expropriate land for its water tasks only. Of the 30 seats on its general board, 26 are for residents, two for unbuilt land and two for nature; of the residents' seats BBB now holds 7, Partij voor Zeeland and the SGP 4 each, the CDA, the PvdA, Water Natuurlijk and the VVD 2 each, and the Algemene Waterschapspartij, the ChristenUnie and the Partij voor de Dieren 1 each; ZLTO fills both seats for unbuilt land, and one of them sits on the daily board, responsible for fresh water, salinisation and drought. Score 5: it decides binding rules for the island's farms.
attributes.affected: Salinisation and drought enter its tasks: with sea level rise, drought and subsidence, more of its area may come to face salinisation; drought strengthens the harm saline seepage does, which is hard to undo; and drought, warming and salinisation affect the ecology of its waters. Dry springs and summers showed farming's need for fresh water in those seasons: supplying it is no legal duty of the board, yet a clear need in society, which it answers within its core tasks, using its surface water system to counter drought and keep fresh water available, exploring its treatment plants' effluent as a source and the sustainable use of fresh groundwater. Its budget for fresh water is limited, the costs fall to whoever benefits, and its legal means to charge them are limited. To make the use of groundwater more sustainable it needs better monitoring, research and groundwater models, and better permits, supervision and enforcement, since extracting too much too fast draws up the salt water under the fresh water; where too little fresh water is available, drying can damage roads, nature and dikes.

attributes.label: Gemeente  Schouwen-Duiveland
attributes.interest: A vital and liveable countryside, with farming, one of the island's main economic pillars, made climate-proof against salinisation, subsidence and extreme weather, and a reliable water system; water basins on farmland fitted into the landscape.
attributes.influence: Its council sets the omgevingsplan, since 1 January 2024 the one plan for the use of all land and buildings on the island, farmland included, and may expropriate land for a use that plan allows, where that is necessary and urgent, and establish a right of first refusal on land given a non-agricultural function; its executive decides where a farm may build a water basin outside its building plot; it pays part of farms' advice, research and machines for fresh water and climate-proof farming, and leads the Living Lab Schouwen-Duiveland. Score 5: it decides binding plans for the island's farms.
attributes.affected: Salinisation, subsidence and extreme weather put pressure on farming, one of the island's main economic pillars, and with it on the vital and liveable countryside the municipality seeks to keep. It budgets €1.1 million for a new Living Lab programme (2025), so that the farm sector stays diverse and resilient; its subsidy for farms' advice, research and machines for fresh water opens on 1 October 2026. The water basins farms build against drought damage have a spatial impact on the landscape, so the municipality sets how a basin outside a building plot is fitted into it.

attributes.label: Provincie Zeeland
attributes.interest: Keeping agriculture in the delta, for the fertile deltas' part in world food production, and strengthening nature; enough fresh water and good water quality, worked out with stakeholders in the Zeeuws Deltaplan Zoet Water; groundwater extraction in balance with its recharge.
attributes.influence: Sets regional water policy and the omgevingsverordening, whose rules reach the water board, the municipalities, residents and businesses, among them instruction rules the water board's water level plans and the municipality's omgevingsplan follow; sets the water board's tasks and rules of organisation and supervises it, its executive able to annul any of the board's decisions; designates in the omgevingsverordening the waters that need a water level plan; grants the permits for groundwater extraction above 150,000 m³ a year, for drinking water and for open soil energy systems. It may take project decisions and, for a provincial interest or where that is efficient, expropriate land, and for a provincial interest establish a right of first refusal on land given a non-agricultural function. In its omgevingsverordening it may rank the uses within the two lowest categories of the verdringingsreeks; no source read shows Zeeland doing so. It commissioned a study of a fresh water pipeline to the island (2021), after the farming sector pressed for one; the study leaves open who pays and who would run it, and no source read shows a decision on a route. Score 5: it decides binding rules for the island's farms, mostly through the water board's and the municipality's decisions.
attributes.affected: Zeeland has very little supply of fresh water of its own and salinisation as a specific concern; climate change raises the chance that demand for fresh water outruns supply, with negative consequences for agricultural yields and nature values, against its aim of keeping agriculture in the delta. Long drought causes water shortages, and sea level rise more (saline) seepage. Farms' groundwater extraction bears on its policy of balance between extraction and recharge: it researches registering extractions and extends the groundwater monitoring network to follow the small fresh groundwater stocks better.

attributes.label: Banks lending to the  island's farmers
attributes.interest: Loans a farm can repay from its cash flow, with its land and other assets as security; an investment whose returns are not yet proven they often count as a risk. In Rabobank's words, to be a partner of the entrepreneur and help farmers invest in sustainability.
attributes.influence: Supply 90% of the borrowed capital of Dutch farms (2018), Rabobank about 85% of the lending to the Dutch food and agri sector (2021); they decide whether a farm gets a loan and at what rate, judging more and more by its cash flow and the entrepreneur, as the Basel capital rules steer them towards profitability and liquidity, with land still an important security, and they count sustainability in classifying a borrower. Measured nationally: no source shows the banks' shares on the island. Score 4: they decide credit many of the island's farms depend on, without binding them.
attributes.affected: Of the Netherlands' arable regions, the south-western clay region faces the greatest task with drought in Rabobank's research (2023), above all because Zeeland is relatively vulnerable to salinisation: the average arable farm's income has held up in dry years, higher prices outweighing lower yields, but farms with little access to fresh water or with salinisation problems can come under pressure, and less fresh water could force a switch to far costlier drip irrigation. Measured for the whole bank, Rabobank's provisions for expected credit losses carry an adjustment for rising climate and environmental risks, more probable and intense droughts and floods among them, €87 million at the end of 2024 (€14 million a year earlier), its climate-sensitive sectors judged on five events, drought and water scarcity among them; no source read shows the banks' risk on the island.

attributes.label: Buyers and processors  of the island's crops
attributes.interest: Raw material of the volume and quality their plants and customers need. Cosun Beet Company, owned by its growers as a cooperative, wants the most value from the beet and good long-term returns for its members, its production in balance with its sales; a potato processor secures its supply through contracts that fix a volume and often its price.
attributes.influence: Decide what they take from the island's farms, at what price and to what quality. Cosun Beet Company, part of Royal Cosun, the growers' cooperative that also owns the potato processor Aviko, processes all sugar beet grown in the Netherlands: it sets how much beet each member may deliver (for 2026 cut from 100% to 90% of the allocation, after high yields and with sales limited) and advises its growers field by field. The Dutch potato processing industry turns about 4 million tonnes of potatoes a year into frozen products, an estimated 80% of them exported; of the potatoes for the industry, 5 to 10% are sold free and the rest under contract or in a pool (2020, pp. 1, 7, 11–12), a contract fixing a quantity, a price or both, the common hectare-tonnage contract a volume per hectare besides the price, with bonuses for quality and grading and deductions for tare; Aviko, Farm Frites, Lamb Weston/Meijer and McCain are the processors whose contract prices are reported. Measured nationally: no source read shows which buyers take the island's potatoes, onions and vegetables, or their shares there. No source read shows a buyer building, keeping or closing a plant for new crops on or near the island. Score 4: they decide the sales many of the island's farms depend on (in 2025, 120 of its 240 farms grew potatoes and 110 sugar beet), without binding them.
attributes.affected: In a drought their supply shrinks and its quality falls, measured nationally: in 2018 the Dutch harvest was expected to be 23% smaller for potatoes, 13% for sugar beet and 44% for onions than a year earlier (CBS's estimate from a survey of 5,000 farmers), and north-western Europe's potato yield at least 15 to 25% below the long-term average. About 80% of the Dutch potato crop is sold to processors under contract, at around nine cents a kilo in 2018, while free-market potatoes reached 30 cents; many growers expected not to deliver their contracted volume, and growers asked the processors to share the cost of extra irrigation and to accept force majeure, while the processors held that a grower under contract should irrigate. Processors want potatoes of at least 40 mm, which many would not reach, and the potatoes' very high dry matter risked damage at harvest. No source read shows how salinisation on the island affects the buyers and processors.

attributes.label: ZLTO
attributes.interest: The continuity of farming and horticulture and a future for farmers and growers. On the island, more fresh water: in its island branch's words (2023), catching more rain and a collective system that brings fresh water to the island, a pipeline from the Haringvliet shared among the farmers.
attributes.influence: The association of 11,500 farmers and growers in Zeeland, Noord-Brabant and Zuid-Gelderland, in 44 local branches that speak for their members to the municipality and the water board; its board appoints the two members for unbuilt land, farmland included, of the water board's general board of 30, one of whom sits on its daily board, responsible for fresh water, salinisation and drought; it takes the initiative in the plan that carries out the Deltaplan Agrarisch Waterbeheer in Zeeland, with the water board and the province; on the island its branch looks for more fresh water with the municipality and the province, and Delphy's report on the island's freshwater demand (2023), whose conclusions the branch welcomed, finds that farming there becomes impossible without more fresh water. Its island branch has called a pipeline from the Haringvliet the one solution (2023). In Reimerswaal, elsewhere in Zeeland, a request from its local branch to the water board and the province (2020) started the study of an extended fresh water supply, and it is a party to the intention agreement on that supply (2025), leading the work of gaining the farmers' support for it. Score 3: it shapes the water board's, the municipality's and the province's decisions directly by representing farmers, binding none.
attributes.affected: Its members' farms bear the losses: in a ZLTO board member's words (2022), drought and heat would make Zeeland's potato harvest considerably smaller than normal, and the drought, the article adds, salinised farmland, which harms crops; its island branch's chair (2023) expects the farms still active there in 2030 to have almost no income. It answers by asking for fresh water collectively: storage for rain, and pipelines from the rivers to farmland, which need large investments and more from the national government.

attributes.label: Consumers
attributes.interest: Food that is affordable, tastes good, is safe and of a known origin: across the EU, cost (54%), taste (51%), food safety and origin (both 46%) are the factors most often chosen when buying food; in the Netherlands nutrient content comes first (62%), and its impact on the environment and climate is chosen by 29%, among the highest shares in the EU (2022).
attributes.influence: What they buy reaches the island's farms through the buyers and processors: in the Netherlands about 4 million tonnes of potatoes a year become about 2 million tonnes of frozen products, an estimated 80% exported, sold through catering and fast food worldwide; when these closed in the Covid-19 crisis (2020), the market for processing potatoes collapsed mid-season, with about 1.5 million tonnes left in growers' stores. Dutch household consumption of table potatoes fell 15% from 2014 to 2017, to 13 kg a person, and Dutch production of table potatoes with it, to about 450,000 tonnes a year. Measured nationally. Score 2: they shape the farms' decisions indirectly, through the buyers' demand.
attributes.affected: In the 2018 drought, measured nationally, the potatoes and onions in the shops were smaller but stayed on the shelves. Onions became dearer, a kilo sometimes 25 cents more (LTO Nederland), as their trade rarely uses fixed-price contracts; potatoes, mostly grown under delivery contracts at prices agreed in advance, hardly did, though Albert Heijn saw both slightly dearer, supply being scarcer while demand stayed the same. The supermarkets' trade association expected consumers to notice little and not to eat less. No source read traces an effect on consumers to salinisation on the island.

attributes.label: EU
attributes.interest: Through its Common Agricultural Policy: farmers supported and agricultural productivity improved, for a stable supply of affordable food, a reasonable living for farmers, action on climate change and the sustainable management of natural resources, and living rural areas and landscapes. Through its banking rules: a resilient banking sector, financial stability and stable funding of the economy.
attributes.influence: Its Common Agricultural Policy is managed and funded at European level from the EU budget, through two funds: the EAGF, for direct support and market measures, and the EAFRD, for rural development, €387 billion for 2021–2027. Each EU country draws up a national CAP Strategic Plan from the toolbox of measures the Commission provides, and its payments are managed nationally, in the Netherlands by RVO at the tariffs LVVN's minister sets. To receive EU income support, farmers must respect conditionality: the statutory management requirements, EU rules on public, animal and plant health, animal welfare and the environment that bind every farmer, and the good agricultural and environmental conditions that bind those receiving CAP support; a farmer who violates them has the support reduced. EU funding for rural development co-funded the Living Lab's Samenwerken voor Zoet Water (2020–2022) and paid half of its drainage demonstrations on three of the island's farms (2022–2024). Its banking package (CRR III/CRD VI) puts the final elements of the Basel III standards of 2017 into EU law, the new Capital Requirements Regulation rules applying from 1 January 2025. Score 5: it decides binding rules for the island's farms, through conditionality.
attributes.affected: In the Commission's words (2025), water scarcity already affects 30% of Europe's land area every year, and extreme weather, persistent droughts among it, will only worsen as the effects of climate change grow, affecting citizens, agriculture, the environment and businesses, with effects on health and on the supply of energy, food and drinking water, and leading more and more to economic losses across the EU. Its Water Resilience Strategy (2025) answers with, among other measures, a recommendation to improve water efficiency in the EU by at least 10% by 2030, each Member State setting its own targets, and a strengthened real-time early-warning and monitoring system for floods and droughts. Measured EU-wide: no source read shows how salinisation on the island affects the EU.

attributes.label: LVVN
attributes.interest: Sustainable, sufficient and safe food on everyone's plate, valuable nature and a vital countryside, for present and future generations. Agriculture, nature and food quality strengthen each other and sometimes chafe; it makes those dilemmas open to discussion and looks for ways forward together with others in society.
attributes.influence: Makes national policy, laws and rules for agriculture, fisheries, food and nature, whose compliance the NVWA supervises. Its minister sets the tariffs of the EU's Common Agricultural Policy support in the Netherlands: for 2025, €174 per hectare of basic income support, €50.35 more on a farm's first 40 hectares, and an eco-scheme premium of €60, €100 or €200 per hectare. RVO pays them out on its behalf to the farms that apply, in 2026 the eco-scheme premium for activities serving climate, soil and air, water, landscape and biodiversity, to a farm that keeps to the CAP's conditionalities. It publishes the Delta Programme with IenW and VRO, has directors on the Bestuurlijk Platform Zoetwater that advises the minister of IenW on the Delta Programme for Fresh Water, and with IenW and STOWA had a knowledge programme on salt in agriculture, nature and water management drawn up by Deltares, KWR and others, on the salt tolerance of crops among its questions: its plan estimates €760,000 for the first year, and €400,000 was available in 2025 to start carrying it out. Measured nationally: no source read shows its payments on the island. Score 3: it funds the island's farms directly, through the CAP payments.
attributes.affected: Drought and salinisation hit the farming its policy is for. Measured nationally by the Algemene Rekenkamer (2026), over 1998–2023, drought lowers the yield of potatoes by 1 to 2.1% a year on average, of arable vegetables, mainly onions, by 1.1 to 2.7%, of cereals by 0.9 to 2.1% and of sugar beet by 1.5 to 1.6%, from the province with the least damage to the one with the most; for ware potatoes the national 2.1% came in 2023 to 70.5 million kg and €14 to €35 million less; and drought raises salinisation, with effects on agriculture and nature. With IenW and STOWA it had a knowledge programme on salt drawn up (2025), because the growing salinisation of water and soil, partly through climate change, raises questions that need fundamental gaps in knowledge filled: how salty the soil moisture becomes, and how salt-tolerant crops are under Dutch conditions: when salt damages them and how far they recover. No source read shows how salinisation on the island affects LVVN.

attributes.label: IenW
attributes.interest: A reachable country with strong dikes, where people stay safe and get from A to B, with clean air, soil and water, its living environment cared for and raw materials used sparingly. For fresh water, the goal it set with the regional governments in 2019: in 2050 the Netherlands is resilient against freshwater shortage.
attributes.influence: Responsible for national water policy, the safety, quality and availability of water among it, and for the working of Dutch water management as a whole; manages the main water system, the large rivers, lakes and seas, with Rijkswaterstaat carrying it out; may instruct provinces and water boards on regional water management where international obligations or interests beyond a region require it. Its freshwater policy ranks the uses of water in a shortage by the verdringingsreeks, which every water manager follows: agriculture in the last of its four categories, temporary irrigation of capital-intensive crops one higher. Its minister coordinates the Delta Programme for Fresh Water, which the six freshwater regions carry out, and manages the Delta Fund, which pays all of Rijkswaterstaat's freshwater measures in the main water system and 25% of a region's (up to 50% for innovative ones or those of several regions): just over €58 million for fresh water in 2026; early in 2027 the Rijk and the regions set the measures for 2028–2033. The Delta Programme 2027, which its minister presents to parliament with the Delta Fund's budget, proposes for the south-west delta that the areas with no supply from outside speed up their way to self-sufficiency, with no extra demand on the Hollandsch Diep and Haringvliet. Score 2: it shapes the island's adaptation through the province, the water board and Rijkswaterstaat; no source read shows the Delta Fund paying for a measure on the island.
attributes.affected: Drought brings freshwater shortages its policy must answer, measured nationally: in the Algemene Rekenkamer's report (2026), the 2018 drought did €450 million to €2.08 billion of economic damage in the Netherlands (Ecorys, 2019), and in the KNMI's scenarios an extremely dry summer of today will be an average summer in the future. The Rekenkamer finds that the Delta Programme for Fresh Water, which IenW's minister coordinates, has no concrete, measurable goal, so whether it is on schedule for 2050 cannot be judged; nearly three quarters of the measures studied ran 2.4 to 3 years late, and the first phase's spending, €512.5 million, came 40% above the €364.7 million estimated; while measures are delayed, the damage of drought persists. In the cabinet's reaction to the Delta Programme 2027, the Netherlands had a considerable water shortage in the summer of 2026, raised on 16 July to drought level 2, an actual water shortage: no social disruption, but damage and hindrance, with several functions and interests under pressure. No source read shows how salinisation on the island affects IenW.

attributes.label: Rijkswaterstaat
attributes.interest: A safe, liveable and reachable Netherlands, worked on together with others; in drought, the little fresh water of the large rivers and lakes divided as well as it can among all who use it.
attributes.influence: Manages the main water system for IenW, the large rivers, lakes and seas, the Delta waters outside the island's dikes among them, for national safety and fresh water supply. In drought it judges, as the water board does for its waters, whether water runs short, and divides the fresh water of the Rhine and Meuse through weirs, pumping stations and sluices by the verdringingsreeks. Most of Zeeland lies outside the area it can supply, where users depend on rain and groundwater; the island has no fresh water supplied from outside (the municipality, 2023). A pipeline to the island, which the province had explored (2021), would draw on waters it manages: the Volkerak-Zoommeer, at the Noorder Krammer or the Schelde-Rijnkanaal, or the Haringvliet, the study's most future-proof source. Score 2: it shapes the island's adaptation indirectly, through what a supply route could draw on; none exists.
attributes.affected: Drought and salinisation fall on the main water system it manages: as the summer precipitation deficit grows, the possibility of supplying fresh water through the large rivers shrinks (IPLO, 2025). The Algemene Rekenkamer (2026) expects lower river discharges, above all in summer, more and more often, so shipping suffers drought damage more often, and a growing demand for extra flushing against salinisation; at low water levels ships sail with less load, cargo is spread over more ships and waits at the locks grow longer. When less water is available than is needed, it must divide the little fresh water there is by the verdringingsreeks. The Rekenkamer recommends that IenW's minister commission it explicitly as the executor of the Delta Programme's measures in the main water system. No source read shows how salinisation on the island affects Rijkswaterstaat, which supplies no water there.

attributes.label: Delta Climate Center
attributes.interest: Regional transitions towards sustainable, climate-resilient and prosperous deltas, in Zeeland and worldwide, with Zeeland as its living lab.
attributes.influence: A partnership of six knowledge institutes, Scalda, HZ University of Applied Sciences, University College Roosevelt, NIOZ, Utrecht University and Wageningen University & Research, at the Kenniswerf in Vlissingen, which started in mid-2023 with a budget of €88 million from the national government and the province, part of the national compensation package Wind in de Zeilen. Its themes for the Zeeland delta are sustainable food, water safety and water availability, and circularity, with three iconic projects from 2024: Delta Protein, the protein transition, mainly marine; Flexible Deltas, flood-defence landscapes that also offer a future for agriculture, salinisation and freshwater availability among their challenges, with living labs on the Westerschelde, the Oosterschelde (from the second half of 2025) and the coastal zone; and ProceZ. Score 1: no source read shows it working on Schouwen-Duiveland or with the island's farmers.
attributes.affected: In its own words, sea level rise, salinisation and drought are among the consequences of climate change noticeable in delta areas such as Zeeland, and it develops knowledge and innovations to keep them safe and flourishing. In its project Flexible Deltas, salinisation and freshwater availability are among the challenges of flood-defending landscapes, from the forelands to the polders behind the dikes, beside water safety, ecological functions and economic interests, which call for an integrated approach. Measured for Zeeland and the Southwest Delta: no source read shows how salinisation on the island, or its farms' adaptation, affects the DCC.
attributes.ask actors: Delta Climate Center, through DCC: Which Zeeland partners take part in Flexible Deltas' Oosterschelde living lab, and whether the DCC works with the water board, the municipality, ZLTO or the island's farmers.
attributes.no relations: Its own pages (home, About us, Research, Flexible Deltas) and NIOZ's news of its start (2023) name none it holds toward an actor on this map: they name its six founding institutes, and its partners in Zeeland only as government bodies, nature and landscape organisations, businesses, umbrella organisations and local communities; none shows it working on Schouwen-Duiveland or with the island's farmers. The province's funding of it is the province's relation.

attributes.label: Deltares
attributes.interest: Applied research on water and the subsurface, for future, sustainable and safe deltas and a resilient infrastructure.
attributes.influence: An independent knowledge institute for applied research on water and the subsurface, working with governments, companies, knowledge institutions, universities and NGOs in the Netherlands and abroad. On the island it carried out, with KWR, Acacia Water, Agrarisch Schouwen-Duiveland and the municipality, the Living Lab's project Samenwerken voor Zoet Water (2020–2022), paid by the EU's rural development fund, the province and the municipality, whose quickscans gave 13 farmers advice on storing fresh water that fits the farm's soil, groundwater and economics, followed by five feasibility studies for groups of farms; drainage and infiltration, it concludes, can store far more fresh water underground than was thought; it wrote the project's final report for the municipality with KWR, Acacia Water and Buro Waterfront. With Acacia Water, Delphy, the trial farm Rusthoeve and the municipality it had anti-salinisation and double drainage on the low-lying poelgronden of three farms, at Kerkwerve and Dreischor, demonstrated and monitored (drains laid in 2022, closing meeting in 2024), half paid by the EU; with KWR and WUR it carried out LN2050, research on a climate- and water-robust layout of the countryside towards 2050, the island one of its three example areas, for its farmers, ZLTO's island branch and the Zeeland governments, part of the Ministry of Economic Affairs' Knowledge and Innovation Agenda; in 2025 it was among the knowledge institutes carrying out the national knowledge programme on salt. Score 3: the project's advice reached the participating farms directly; no source read says which partner wrote which advice.
attributes.affected: Salinisation raises knowledge questions it is among those answering: in 2025 it was among the knowledge institutes carrying out the national programme on dealing with salt in agriculture, nature and water management, which LVVN, IenW and STOWA had drawn up because the growing salinisation of water and soil, partly through climate change, raises such questions, to fill fundamental gaps in knowledge, how salty the soil moisture becomes and how salt-tolerant crops are under Dutch conditions, and to make the answers usable in practice in models and tools; €400,000 was available for 2025, and the partners intend to find about €1 million a year for the whole multi-year programme (IPLO, 2025). On the island, the report it wrote with KWR and Acacia Water (Kaandorp et al., 2022) finds the farms' hesitation to invest working both ways: as long as the measures' costs, risks and gain in yield stay uncertain, farmers do not invest, and as long as they do not invest, the techniques are not refined, nothing is learned from building them, their effects cannot be monitored, and no knowledge base forms at agricultural advisory firms and contractors with which the cost of advice and building could fall; it recommends pilots with monitoring, and more research on the measures' economic feasibility. Following the report, it took part in drainage demonstrations on three of the island's farms (2022–2024). The EU paid half of their cost and the province and the municipality a large part, beside an own contribution from the participating knowledge parties.

attributes.label: Acacia Water
attributes.interest: Access to clean and safe fresh water for everyone.
attributes.influence: An independent water consultancy, based in Gouda, with 41 employees and work in 19 countries, water for agriculture and groundwater development among its expertise. On the island its hydrologists led farmers in measuring the salinity of the ditches round their fields (Natuurlijk Zoet, 2019–2021, set up with Agrarisch Schouwen-Duiveland and the water board, the results in the water board's database); it carried out, with Deltares, KWR, Agrarisch Schouwen-Duiveland and the municipality, the Living Lab's project Samenwerken voor Zoet Water (2020–2022), paid by the EU's rural development fund, the province and the municipality, whose quickscans gave 13 farmers advice on storing fresh water that fits the farm's soil, groundwater and economics, followed by five feasibility studies for groups of farms; drainage and infiltration, it concludes, can store far more fresh water underground than was thought, and co-wrote its final report for the municipality; with Deltares, Delphy, the trial farm Rusthoeve and the municipality it had anti-salinisation and double drainage on the low-lying poelgronden of three farms, at Kerkwerve and Dreischor, demonstrated and monitored (drains laid in 2022, closing meeting in 2024), half paid by the EU. Score 3: the project's advice reached the participating farms directly; no source read says which partner wrote which advice.
attributes.affected: In its own words, a rising demand for water and climate change threaten the availability of fresh water for communities, farmers and countries. On the island, the report it wrote with Deltares and KWR (Kaandorp et al., 2022) finds the farms' hesitation to invest working both ways: as long as the measures' costs, risks and gain in yield stay uncertain, farmers do not invest, and as long as they do not invest, the techniques are not refined, nothing is learned from building them, their effects cannot be monitored, and no knowledge base forms at agricultural advisory firms and contractors with which the cost of advice and building could fall; it recommends pilots with monitoring, and more research on the measures' economic feasibility. Following the report, it took part in drainage demonstrations on three of the island's farms (2022–2024). The EU paid half of their cost and the province and the municipality a large part, beside an own contribution from the participating knowledge parties.

attributes.label: Delphy
attributes.interest: Healthy, successful and sustainable cultivation: better performance for growers, through research, data-driven crop management, advice and training.
attributes.influence: A knowledge company, part of Peterson Solutions, with more than 250 professionals active in over 60 countries and its address in Wageningen; its crop experts advise growers in every plant sector, arable farming among them. It is among the Living Lab's partners, its manager for arable farming and field vegetables in the south-west and two soil and water experts among the partners, and with Acacia Water, Deltares, the trial farm Rusthoeve and the municipality it had anti-salinisation and double drainage on the low-lying poelgronden of three farms, at Kerkwerve and Dreischor, demonstrated and monitored (drains laid in 2022, closing meeting in 2024), half paid by the EU. In 2023 it carried out the study of the island's freshwater demand, commissioned and paid for by ZLTO's island branch, Agrarisch Schouwen-Duiveland, with funding from the municipality and the Zuidwestelijke Delta: farming on the island becomes impossible without more fresh water, since the current freshwater measures and innovations supply too little, fit only part of the island, are costly and have not yet proven their value, so a supply of fresh water stays needed and more rain must be stored; ZLTO's island branch draws from it that a supply of fresh water is unavoidable. Score 2: the demonstrations give data on the techniques' effects, and its study informs the island's debate on fresh water; no source read shows it advising individual farms.
attributes.affected: It took part in drainage demonstrations on three of the island's farms (2022–2024). The EU paid half of their cost and the province and the municipality a large part, beside an own contribution from the participating knowledge parties. No source read shows how salinisation on the island, or its farms' adaptation, affects Delphy otherwise.

attributes.label: Breeders and trading  houses of seed  potatoes
attributes.interest: New varieties with the traits their salespeople find most important: one trading house, endorsed by another, asks them once a year for the ten most important aspects of a new variety, and salt tolerance is not yet among them; many of the 32 people interviewed, experts, farmers and policymakers among them, want an official label for salt tolerance, whose absence leads to unsubstantiated claims (interviews, about 2020). The salt-tolerant seed potatoes bred in the Netherlands are mostly for export to arid countries such as Egypt and Morocco, stakeholders in the Dutch potato industry say.
attributes.influence: Decide which potato varieties reach the island's farmers, and so the CLD's Yield of salt-tolerant varieties on offer: Dutch breeders and suppliers sell cultivars that differ in salt tolerance, measured in field trials on Texel (2012–2018); with no official label for it, trading houses claim salt tolerance for no variety, one of them saying only which suit saline soils best and worst. Conventional breeding typically takes 10 to 15 years. Measured nationally. Score 3: they shape the farms' choice of variety directly, binding none; no source read shows the island's farms growing a salt-tolerant variety.
attributes.affected: No source read traces an effect on them to salinisation on the island.
attributes.no relations: No source read shows their trade with an actor on this map: the sources read show their cultivars tested on Texel and their trading houses' view of salt tolerance, measured nationally.

attributes.label: Nature managers on the  island  (Natuurmonumenten,  Staatsbosbeheer)
attributes.interest: More water in its nature areas, and more of it held there, in Natuurmonumenten's words (2023): the longer dry periods from spring into summer now cause the problems, and it raised the thought of bridging the long road to more durable solutions with emergency provisions, freshwater buffers of 5 to 10 ha, at pumping stations for example, for the next ten years, where the demand of farming, recreation and nature could come together. No source read states Staatsbosbeheer's interest.
attributes.influence: The largest managers of the island's nature areas (2023). On its south coast, in Plan Tureluur, Staatsbosbeheer manages the western Prunje areas and the eastern ones towards Zierikzee were to come to Natuurmonumenten; a seepage ditch rings the whole area, so that its higher water level does not add seepage on the land around it (2006). Both were interviewed as the island's nature managers for KWR's exploration of a climate- and water-robust island (2026). Score 2: their areas border the farmland, and their wish for more water held there bears on the island's fresh water; no source read shows them deciding a measure for the farms.
attributes.affected: Drought: in the summer of 2022 the island's thousands of breeding pairs raised almost no young, in Natuurmonumenten's words (2023).
attributes.ask actors: Nature managers on the island (Natuurmonumenten, Staatsbosbeheer), through DCC or Living Lab: Whether the province pays Natuurmonumenten and Staatsbosbeheer for managing their areas on the island through its nature subsidies, and whether that money sets the water levels those areas need.
attributes.no relations: No source read shows a relation it holds toward another actor on this map: Natuurmonumenten's shared buffers are a thought (2023), and the source on the seepage ditch (2006) names no actor that keeps it. The water levels in their areas, which the water board sets agreed with them, are the water board's relation.

attributes.label: Living Lab  Schouwen-Duiveland
attributes.interest: Parties innovating together, so that the island's move to climate-adaptive, self-sufficient (ground)water management goes faster; in the municipality's new programme (2025), a farm sector that stays diverse and resilient.
attributes.influence: A network with a light organisation, led by the municipality, which started officially in January 2019 as a place for parties who want to innovate together; the water board, the province and Agrarisch Schouwen-Duiveland are among its initiators and core partners, Delphy and the trial farm Rusthoeve among its partners. Its project Samenwerken voor Zoet Water (2020–2022), carried out with Deltares, KWR, Acacia Water, Agrarisch Schouwen-Duiveland and the municipality and paid by the EU's rural development fund, the province and the municipality, made quickscans for 13 farmers and feasibility studies for groups of farms; a later project demonstrated and monitored new drainage on three of the island's farms, at Kerkwerve and Dreischor (2022–2024), half paid by the EU. The municipality budgets €1.1 million for its new programme (2025). Score 3: its projects shape the farms' storage decisions directly, through advice and demonstrations on their land, binding none.
attributes.affected: It was set up for the question: the island's move to a climate-adaptive water system can only happen with the municipality, the water board, farmers, advisers, experts and knowledge institutions working together, and the Living Lab was set up to help speed it up.

attributes.label: Agrarisch  Schouwen-Duiveland
attributes.interest: More fresh water for the island's farms: in its words (2023), catching more rain and a collective system that brings fresh water to the island, a pipeline from the Haringvliet shared among the farmers.
attributes.influence: ZLTO's branch on the island, one of its 44 local branches that speak for their members to the municipality and the water board, with a board of its own and an arable farmer as its chair. It commissioned and paid for Delphy's study of the island's freshwater demand (2023), whose interim results were presented to its members, and after it called a pipeline from the Haringvliet the one solution (2023); its chair looks for more fresh water with the municipality and the province (2026). It is one of the Living Lab's initiators and core partners, and carried out its project Samenwerken voor Zoet Water (2020–2022) with Deltares, KWR, Acacia Water and the municipality. Score 3: it shapes the municipality's, the province's and the water board's decisions directly by representing the island's farmers, binding none.
attributes.affected: Its members' farms bear the losses: the study it commissioned finds farming on the island impossible without more fresh water (2023), and in 2026 its chair, a potato grower, lost a fifth of his harvest to drought and had stopped growing onions for want of fresh water.

attributes.description: A higher sea raises the water pressure in the sand below the clay, so more salt groundwater seeps up and the ditches get saltier; in the fields the drains will probably catch most of the effect (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 11, for Schouwen-Duiveland). The rise in pressure fades quickly with distance from the coast (de Louw et al., 2011, p. 3674): in a model of the western Netherlands around Amsterdam, The Hague, Rotterdam and Utrecht, it reached up to 10 km from the coast and the main rivers, and 5 km inland it was about 40% of the rise (Oude Essink et al., 2010, pp. 3, 9). How much of the rise reaches the dikes along the Grevelingen, which has no tide, the sources read do not say. Within the year: the seepage follows the water pressures, which change constantly (de Louw et al., 2011, p. 3675).

attributes.description: More winter rain gives the drains more to carry off: tile drains usually discharge the shallow groundwater quickly during rain, as other studies found (de Louw et al., 2011, p. 3661), and on Schouwen-Duiveland enough rain falls over the year, but a large part of it is drained away in the wet season (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 54), a figure for the whole island, which the link reads for the low polders, whose drained rain the variable counts. attributes.description: Where the lens is thin, saline groundwater lies just below the roots and reaches the root zone by capillary rise. In the island's low polders with saline seepage the lens is about 2 m thick, its mixing zone in the clay top layer, and capillary rise of saline groundwater is very likely now, possibly damaging crops (de Louw et al., 2011, pp. 3667, 3673, 3675, measured on Schouwen-Duiveland); the topsoil there is fresh thanks to the rainwater lens, which makes farming possible, and these low polders of heavy clay make up a large part of the island (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 4, 10). On Duiveland the salt water reaches into or almost into the root zone in places (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, p. 26). Within the year: in a dry season, with the groundwater below the drains, the flow there is only upward (de Louw et al., 2011, p. 3673).

attributes.description: The thinner the lens under the well, the sooner the salt below reaches it: in the Freshmaker pilot at Ovezande, Zuid-Beveland, the pumped water grew saltier late in each pumping season, which the report explains by the lens thinning as fresh water is pumped, so that upconing could reach the shallow well (Oude Essink et al., 2018, p. 67). Zeeland's water board lets farms pump without a permit where its map shows a fresh groundwater body outside its vulnerable areas, one at least 15 m thick or reaching the geohydrological base (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2026f, arts. 1.1 and 4.8 b). Measured on a creek ridge elsewhere in Zeeland, a lens like those under the island's creek ridges (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 10). Within the year.

attributes.description: Holds in the low polders, where the thin rainwater lens keeps the topsoil fresh, which makes farming possible there (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 10, for the island): water anti-salinisation drainage keeps in the lens reaches only the crop on that field, as groundwater and soil moisture, and is expected to lie too deep for its roots at germination (p. 33), when drought mostly falls for the farmers of the low polders (pp. 27, 31); later in the summer the soil supplies a well-established crop (p. 27). The same report rates the crop's use of that water as possibly low in efficiency, as part of it can flow away, and as not steerable, since it sits in the field (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 33, from feasibility studies of five farm clusters in the low polders). In Zeeland the water board's general rule lets farms pump fresh groundwater for irrigation of more than 10 m³ an hour, up to 60 m³ an hour, 3,000 m³ a quarter and 8,000 m³ a year, without a permit but notified at least four weeks ahead, through a horizontal well, from a fresh body its map shows outside its vulnerable areas, one at least 15 m thick or reaching the geohydrological base (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2026f, arts. 1.1, 2.9 lid 2 h and 4.8 b and f), and on the creek ridges some farmers take water from the ridge through a deep drain (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 38), one farm using two to irrigate in summer (p. 40), which is Groundwater extraction for irrigation → Freshwater availability for crops. Within the season.

attributes.description: Salt in the root zone puts sodium (Na+) on the clay in place of calcium (Ca2+); once fresh water washes the salt out, clay that holds much sodium disperses: its aggregates and pores collapse, with troubles to be expected above 1 m.e. of exchangeable sodium per 100 g of dry soil (van Beekom et al., 1953b, pp. 225–226, 230). The delay is on the way back: structure begins to decline in the first winter after the salt leaches out, but the clay only recovers as calcium replaces the sodium again, about 0.7 m.e. Na per 100 g a year in the top 10 cm of soil with calcium carbonate, which takes 5 to 10 years on heavy clay and about a year on very light soil, while soil without it is expected to recover more slowly (van Beekom et al., 1953b, pp. 226–228, after the 1944–45 inundations in Zeeland). Seawater flooding is a much larger salt dose than seepage; soils that took up less sodium recover faster, and no source read shows how much sodium the island's seepage puts on its clay. The only island measurements found lie below the plough layer, to which the loss of crumb structure is confined (van Beekom et al., 1953b, p. 226): on a tile-drained agricultural field with permanent saline seepage, sodium made up 9% of the exchangeable cations at 1.6 m between drains and 3% at 3 m near a drain, well below a flooded soil's 21%, the 9% above and the 3% below the roughly 5% at which structure may suffer (Eeman et al., 2017, pp. 225–227, 238–239; van Beekom et al., 1953b, pp. 225–226). A national knowledge agenda judges, from experience within the SALTA knowledge cluster, that salinisation seems so far to cause little damage to soil structure in the Netherlands, where elevated SAR, ESP or CROSS values are usually not determined (Knol et al., 2025, p. 43).
attributes.simplification: Folds Sodium on the clay, a stock between the two: the salt puts sodium on the clay, and the sodium breaks the clay's structure once the salt washes out. The sign is the product of the two steps (+, then −), so no loop through the link changes, and the stock's slowness is the link's delay. What one link distorts: the delay lies on the way back only, the structure beginning to decline in the first winter after the salt leaches out and recovering over years, while the link draws one delay for both ways.

attributes.description: Upward saline seepage keeps the rainwater lens thin. On the island the lens in the seepage areas is mostly under 2 m (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 10), on average 2 m in a helicopter survey of its low polders, its mixing zone in the clay top layer, and it thickens sharply where the flow turns from seepage to infiltration (de Louw et al., 2011, pp. 3673, 3675, measured on the island, the fluxes from the regional groundwater model). That a larger seepage flux gives a thinner lens comes from a model of a tile-drained field built from the island's field data (de Louw et al., 2011, pp. 3671, 3674). In that model the centre of the mixing zone at a drain always stays within 0.1 m of the drain depth, so seepage moves the lens between the drains, and recharge and drainage depth control it alongside seepage (de Louw et al., 2011, pp. 3659, 3671, 3673–3674); in the model a poorly permeable layer below the drains thins the lens between them and one above them thickens it (p. 3674), and unripened clay, a poorly permeable layer, lies close to the surface over a large part of the island (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 32, 55). A delay, its length open: in that model, started fully saline, 30 years of simulation sufficed for every run to become stationary (de Louw et al., 2011, p. 3665), an upper bound; no source read gives how fast the lens follows a change in seepage.

attributes.description: A seedbed in soil with its structure lets the crops germinate better, with less resowing, and yields rise, most for crops sensitive to structure: on flooded clay in Zeeland, plots whose structure gypsum restored yielded up to 15% more sugar beet, 8% more onions and, on heavy clay, up to twice the summer barley, while cereals on light soil gained little (van Beekom et al., 1953b, p. 234, Table 9). Part of the gain is the longer time to work the soil, the link through Spring workability of the fields. Within the year.

attributes.description: Fresh water supplied from outside adds to what crops can draw on: the island's farming depends on the rain that falls and is stored in the root zone or underground, and none is brought in (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 4), which leaves farms short of water in dry periods (p. 8). How much of a supply reaches crops depends on how it is spread: in a design estimate by an engineering consultancy for Provincie Zeeland, a supply through the island's ditches needs 5 m3/s, of which about 2.8 m3/s is pumped back out at the drainage pumping stations (Witteveen+Bos, 2021, p. 40), and it picks up salt from saline seepage on the way (p. 45), to an estimated average of 500 to 800 mg Cl/l at sprinkling against 95 to 500 mg Cl/l at the three sources considered (p. 42), figures the study calls only a very rough indication (pp. 40, 43), above the 300 mg Cl/l damage threshold of salt-sensitive crops (p. 45). A ring pipeline needs 2 m3/s and sprinkles at the source's quality (pp. 42, 45). Within the season.

attributes.description: Active infiltration adds winter water to the lens on the creek ridges and the dunes: the creek-ridge infiltration system raises the groundwater through the drains in winter so the lens grows, on sandy ground that holds a lens (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 20), and the Freshmaker infiltrates winter water through a deep drain while pumping brackish water from below the lens, an option on the island's creek ridges where the lens lies not too deep (pp. 22, 38), both to pump in summer. What limits it on most of the island is fresh water to infiltrate, since the surface water is mostly saline and drain water the likeliest source (pp. 38, 43, 55), and the rules, under which infiltrating needs a permit as a rule (pp. 26, 45, 54–55; Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2026f, art. 4.5 lid 2). Years to a decade, so a delay: on the island's own creek ridge, infiltration with controlled drainage added about 60,000 m³ of fresh water under a 9.5-ha field in ten years and thickened the lens by up to 3.5 m (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 44, a groundwater model of 2020–2050); under a creek ridge on Walcheren, raising the winter water table 0.5 m thickened a 13–15 m lens by 6–8 m in ten years, and the lens had not reached its new thickness yet (Pauw et al., 2015, pp. 1424–1425, 1429, a model result, which transfers since the island's sandy creek ridges also take in rain over saline groundwater: de Louw et al., 2011, p. 3673).
attributes.simplification: Counts a Freshmaker in the low ground between the dunes and the creek ridge, which the study also finds promising where a suitable sand layer lies in the subsoil (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 24), as thickness of this lens: there too it infiltrates winter water above the brackish water it pumps away (p. 22), though off the creek ridges and dunes the element measures. Every loop through the link keeps its polarity and its mechanism, water infiltrated in winter and pumped in summer; what it leaves out is that such a lens lies off the ridges and dunes the element's other links are written for.

attributes.description: Measures in the low polders keep rain in the field instead of draining it off: controlled drainage and anti-salinisation drainage raise the drains' outflow level, so more water stays in the ground of the field (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 17–18, 29, for the island). On the island's trials raising the drains' outflow level did not plainly keep the water in the field: at Kerkwerve raising the control well barely raised the existing drains' level on one strip, so their discharge fell only very slightly (Oude Essink et al., 2018, p. 91), and near Dreischor, where on one of the two anti-salinisation plots the groundwater never rose to the raised outflow level and the drains did not flow, the authors suspect the groundwater flows away elsewhere (van Hateren et al., 2025, p. 58). Double drainage catches rain rather than keeping it in the field: on two pilots near Kerkwerve its shallow drains carried off 43 to 52% of the winter's net rain to be caught, with little influence on groundwater levels (van Hateren et al., 2025, pp. 4, 77). Within the year.

attributes.description: What farmers pump beyond what the rain puts back thins the lens, the boundary with the saline groundwater below rising: the water board's limit of 800 m³ per hectare a year rests on the balance between recharge by rain, irrigation water and extraction, set to keep the fresh groundwater in stock and the fresh-salt boundary from rising (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2026b), and pumping too fast risks salinisation (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 20–21). Within those rules the effects are meant to stay within the farm's field, with in principle no depletion, and Deltares's modelling of the rules (2018) found that in general they seem enough to prevent strong salinisation under and around the well (Gedeputeerde Staten van Zeeland, 2021, for Zeeland). How fast the lens responds to pumping, no source read shows. In one pilot at Sirjansland, a deep drain pumped about 4,500 m³ a year for two years from a lens thinner than the 15 m the rules require: after the first season the deep monitoring wells showed no salinisation at the bottom or edge of the lens, and after the second geophysical measurements showed the EC at 11 m depth rising, possibly a sign that the pumping shifted the fresh-salt boundary, in data strongly affected by the wet years 2023 and 2024 (Acacia Water, n.d., a consultancy testing with the grower whether small lenses can be managed sustainably, funded by the European Commission and the Province of Zeeland). Its model finds the resistance of any separating layers important for the calculated upconing of saline water, with more to pump where it is higher (Acacia Water, n.d.), and under the creek ridges in the east of the island the deeper subsoil to about 25 m is mostly fine sand with local thin clay layers (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 38).

attributes.description: The more a well pumps from the lens, the further salt groundwater rises towards it: in the Freshmaker pilot at Ovezande, Zuid-Beveland, the water pumped from the shallow well grew saltier as each pumping season went on (Oude Essink et al., 2018, p. 67). The report on the island's freshwater measures lists salinisation at too high a pumping rate as a risk of the creek-ridge infiltration system and of underground storage (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 20–21). Within the year: the cone follows the season's pumping.

attributes.description: A larger harvest per hectare raises income at a given price, the price being World prices of conventional crops. The + holds in full where only the island's yield falls, to salt or a local shortage of fresh water. A dry summer across north-west Europe also raises the price, since the harvests there set it: for potatoes, north-west Europe is one market, and their price was highest in the extremely dry 2018 (Janssens et al., 2020, p. 8). Then what a farm loses depends on how it sells: in 2018, higher prices could help onion growers make up for a harvest forecast 44% below the year before, while potato growers mostly held contracts at prices agreed in advance (NOS, 2018), some 80% of the crop at around nine cents a kilo while free-market potatoes reached 30 (DutchNews.nl, 2018); onions are rarely sold under such contracts (Bogosavac, 2018). On the island, a farm with its own stored water can gain from the high prices of a dry year (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 36). Within the year, as the harvest is sold.

attributes.description: A fall in the land's value that has happened, through salt in R8: does a farm whose land lost value object harder to the next plan? Through its solvency, yes (−); where compensation pays more than the land would fetch on the market, the concern may fall instead (+). A hypothesis for the group model building session, with both signs as the question to farmers.
attributes.simplification: Folds Owners' concern about their land's value, which gathered the reasons for objecting: a fall in the land's value, and a plan that would lower it, raised landowning farmers' concern, and the concern raised their objections. The sign is the product of the two steps, so R8 keeps its polarity, and the concern was no actor's decision of its own. A tenant's concern, losing the lease, was never part of it. What it leaves out: why owners object is no variable on the drawing, a question for the group model building session.

attributes.description: With the same debt, a lower land value is a higher debt relative to the farm's assets: land is 70% of an arable farm's balance sheet (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 13), and its rise in value is what made arable farms' solvency 81% in 2018 (p. 21). A high solvency can let a farm borrow more and at a lower rate (p. 19); the debt itself does not shrink when the land loses value. It holds for the land a farm owns: farms owning little of it barely gain from a rising price (p. 26). While land rose the ratio moved little: from 2006 to 2015 Dutch arable farms' balance sheet per farm doubled, mainly through the rise in the land price, while their solvency rose only from 76% to 78% and their bank loans went from just over 5,000 to 10,000 euro per ha, an unchanged 16% share (Silvis et al., 2017, p. 2, national farm accounts). The note was commissioned by a.s.r. vastgoed vermogensbeheer (p. 4). Within the year: the farm accounts value the land each year (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 13).

attributes.description: Soil work for potatoes should not be done when the soil is too wet, which can smear and compact it; for onions, too-wet soil work can keep a well-crumbled seedbed from forming, and in March and April, as the scenarios' rain rises, unfavourable conditions for it may become more likely; where blight cannot be well controlled, as in organic farming, a potato crop is best planted early where the soil allows (Verstand et al., 2021, pp. 25, 27, for the Netherlands, from a cultivation guide, a crop study and an expert). So, by inference from that guide, the more of the rotation they take, the more farmers need fields that dry early in spring. Holding water back longer, as a buffer for dry times, is sometimes hard for farmers who want onto the land with heavy machinery (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021c, p. 44); on Duiveland the board moves to the higher summer level in March and April as the soil work allows (2021a, p. 66). No source read shows how much spring soil work the new crops need: the sign rests on their needing less. Quinoa, one of the new crops, also needs soil work in spring: in the Netherlands it is sown from the end of March to the end of April and needs a fine seed bed (van Loo, 2023, p. 75, by a Wageningen breeder whose group develops quinoa varieties), so the sign holds where the share moves to crops sown in autumn or winter, such as winter wheat, sown from mid-September to early February (Verstand et al., 2021, p. 29), less clearly where it moves to quinoa; and on clay and zavel, the main topsoil of the island's western low polders (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 27), the main soil work for potatoes is often done before winter (Verstand et al., 2021, p. 25). Within the year.

attributes.description: A farm that relies on high margins can give fewer hectares to lower-margin new crops.

More income from the land raises what buyers bid for it, through what they expect an extra hectare to earn an expanding farm over the years of the investment rather than through last year's income (Farjon et al., 2013, box Maximale biedprijs; Silvis & Voskuilen, 2017, pp. 2–3). The + holds beside drivers the island's farms cannot move: since 1970 the nominal Dutch price has risen more than tenfold while net value added rose two- to threefold, carried by scale enlargement and falling interest rates (Farjon et al., 2013, introduction and section Ontwikkeling van de prijs). Across individual land transactions in the Netherlands from 2004 to 2011, the expected revenue from the land had a significant positive effect on the price, beside land regulations, the spatial environment and local market conditions (Boere, 2015, pp. 81, 98). Years: its swings ran over years, the real price rising sharply and then falling by half in the late 1970s and by 30% between 1995 and 2005 (Farjon et al., 2013, section Ontwikkeling van de prijs): a delay.

attributes.description: More income leaves more, after the household's spending and the farm's payment obligations, repayments included, to save for investment; a negative income leaves too little to reserve, and machines then age (Verhagen et al., 2018, pp. 23, 25). A farm with good solvency can probably take up extra credit when its income is negative, the same report judges, and Dutch arable farms averaged close to 80% solvency in 2015, land more than two thirds of their balance sheet (Verhagen et al., 2018, pp. 23, 25; national farm accounts, no figure for the island), so a poor year may shrink what a solvent farm can invest less than its income. A lasting low income is harder to bridge: the bank looks hard at long-term continuity before deferring payments or giving extra credit (Verhagen et al., 2018, p. 28), and in a simulation of banks' credit checks, which base a new loan on the past three years' net cash flow, solvency was the limit in only 1.2% of farm observations and net cash flow in almost all cases (Lamkowsky, 2023, pp. 51–52, 56, 101; Dutch dairy farms, 2009–2017). Within the year: income adds to the savings in the year it is earned.

attributes.description: Capacity to invest decides whether a farm can pay for a storage measure, not whether it wants to.

Capacity to invest decides whether a farm can pay for the switch (new machines, the first years of a new crop), not whether it wants to. The costs of salt-tolerant seed and soil amendments may not make up for the yield and income salt takes in the first years, when setting up costs most, and the benefits are not always obvious in the short term (Deolu-Ajayi et al., 2024, p. 60); farms whose financial buffers shrank in the corona crisis were expected to be less willing to invest, slowing their modernisation and sustainability, and banks often count financing a new concept whose returns are not yet proven as a risk (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 6). For samphire and sea aster the outlet, not only capacity to invest, limits adoption: their food market is small and easily saturated, in the authors' judgement (van den Burg et al., 2024, p. 6), and growers in Zeeland's saline cultivation, eight in all, say there is little room for new entrants, and that making room would also take strong growth of the market for saline vegetables (Delphy, 2023, p. 49, a consultancy report commissioned by Agrarisch Schouwen Duiveland that argues for a freshwater supply, p. 50). Delphy adds that cheaper imports compete and that few of Zeeland's soils suit these crops, but sees openings in high-end restaurants and retail if the season can be lengthened, and in other saline crops less grown abroad (p. 49). Within the year: the crop is chosen each season.

attributes.description: Higher temperatures and drier weather raise evapotranspiration, the water crops use when they have enough, highest in sunny, warm and dry weather (Allen et al., 1998, FAO-56). Once a crop has drawn the root zone down beyond the water it can take up easily, it uses less water than it needs, in proportion to what is left in the root zone (Allen et al., 1998, ch. 8): the shortfall is the part of the demand that rain, soil moisture and irrigation leave unmet, so the more the crops need, the larger it is. On Schouwen-Duiveland's clay a crop that has come up well gets through the summer on the soil's good supply of moisture, so the shortfall falls mostly at germination early in the season, when a small gift of about 20 mm would cover it; onions also need water while they grow (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 27, 31, 38, from talks with the island's farmers). Within the year.
attributes.simplification: Folds the weather's part of what crops need, a step between the two with no actor and no decision: hotter, drier summers raise what crops need, and what they need beyond the water they get is the shortfall. The sign is the product of the two steps (+, then +). Hotter, drier summers is a Constant, so no loop runs through the link. What the crop plan needs is drawn apart, as Water demand of the crop mix; what the link leaves out is that the weather's part runs straight to the shortfall, not through that variable.

attributes.description: Rain, irrigation and capillary rise from the groundwater add water to the root zone and lower its depletion; once the depletion passes the readily available water, the crop uses less water than it needs (Allen et al., 1998, FAO-56 ch. 8, eqs. 84–85, a daily water balance). So the more fresh water crops can draw on, the smaller the shortfall, within the season. On the island's farms a gift of 20 to 25 mm at germination can make the difference where none can be given now (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 27, 55). In the low western polders (Scharendijke–Brouwershaven–Kerkwerve) the farmers in the project's quickscans find drought a problem mainly at germination: once the crop has come up well, the soil's good moisture supply keeps drought damage later in summer limited even in dry years, and waterlogging is often felt as the larger problem (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 27), though a study paid for by the island's farmers' association assumes a much larger water need (Delphy, 2023, p. 40). How much extra water eases also depends on crop and year: raising the water table by subirrigation on a test field at Rusthoeve on Noord-Beveland, on sandy clay (zavel) with saline seepage, raised dry-matter yield against a reference field by 18 % for onions in dry 2022 but by 2 to 7 % for chicory in dry 2020 and for wheat and potato in normal-to-wet 2021 (Terink et al., 2023, p. 44, a trial by KnowH2O and KWR paid for by the province, the water board and the municipality of Noord-Beveland).

attributes.description: Farmers pump more fresh groundwater as the shortfall grows: the water board registered a considerable increase in extractions in recent years, which the more extreme drought certainly influenced, so the volume pumped rises in dry years (Gedeputeerde Staten van Zeeland, 2021, for Zeeland, whose farms pump under the same rules as the island's). On Schouwen-Duiveland the farms get their fresh water from rain and from the fresh groundwater; the shallow groundwater and the surface water hold high salt levels, and no fresh water can be brought in during dry periods (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 8). Without a permit they may pump where the water board's map shows a fresh groundwater body outside its vulnerable areas, one at least 15 m thick or reaching the geohydrological base (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2026f, arts. 1.1 and 4.8 b), which lies under the creek ridges and the dunes (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 10): in the low polders the farmers talked to do not sprinkle, some trying drip irrigation, while on a creek ridge a livestock farmer pumps from two deep drains for grassland in the summer season, more in dry years, and an arable farmer occasionally irrigates about 20 mm at germination, the report not saying where that water comes from (pp. 27–28, 40, 43). So the link runs where a farm has fresh groundwater under it. The rules cap each well's pumping: under Waterschap Scheldestromen's general rule a well may take at most 800 m³ a year per hectare of its parcel (80 mm) and 8,000 m³ a year, a permit with conditions being possible where a well cannot meet them (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2026b, art. 2.9 and its explanation). For the creek ridges of the south-western delta, Deltares researchers presenting a system to enlarge their fresh lenses stated in 2015, under the rules of that time, that irrigation demand already exceeded the permissible extraction, which led to crop damage (Pauw et al., 2015, p. 1415, a statement, not a measurement), so in a dry summer a growing shortfall may end in crop damage rather than in more pumping. Within the year.
