attributes.description: By the water board's rules the level follows the land's use ("peil volgt functie"): the board adapts it to what an area needs (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, p. 5), reading the use from the current land use and from the uses the municipality's land-use plan designates, with what is expected within about five years (p. 7). A plan starts from the optimal level for each use and soil, nature's set with the site managers (2021a, p. 29), and where nature and farmland share a level area on Duiveland the plan keeps nature's level and keeps the farm parcel draining, in one area by linking it to the neighbouring, lower area, in the other by closing a leak (2021a, pp. 61–62). So the less land is farmed as arable land, the more reason for a raise, whoever asks. By the board's own study for its plan, in most of Duiveland's level areas a raise is possible only once the discharge capacity is enlarged, since levels in several are kept low on purpose to store extreme rain (2021a, p. 69), and the province's norm for that storage and discharge capacity, which the board tests against, is the same once in 25 years for arable land and grassland (2021a, pp. 12, 33–34; Provincie Zeeland, 2024, art. 3.3, p. 2), so land that goes from arable crops to grass is held to the same norm as before. In 2026 the board proposed to enlarge Duiveland's discharge capacity against flooding, and its slides give no date (2026a, slides 12, 17), though the province asks the board, as a duty of effort, to meet the norm by 1 January 2028 (Provincie Zeeland, 2024, art. 3.3, p. 2), so whether the limit lifts before 2050 is open. Years, so a delay: the board weighs it as it prepares a plan, which it does when its evaluation every three years finds a plan no longer current, or once a plan is 17 years old (2025, pp. 16–17).

attributes.description: The saltier the field, the fewer of the crops most sensitive to salt a farm keeps: on low fields with strong saline seepage on the island, farmers have stopped growing sensitive crops such as sown onions (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 31). Years, so a delay: salt in a field is largely invisible and seldom measured, a lower yield is hard to put down to it, and interviewees expected it to take more dry summers like 2018 to make salt urgent (Beauchampet, 2022, p. 216, interviews in the salinisation-prone provinces, Zeeland among them).
attributes.simplification: Folds Farmers' experience of damage, a stock that builds over dry summers, into this link's delay: farmers respond to the damage they come to notice, not to the state of the soil. Every loop through the link keeps its polarity and its mechanism, and the delay is kept; what it leaves out is how far what farmers notice differs from what the soil shows.

attributes.description: The margin given up is net of what the new crop earns, a margin being revenue minus the crop's variable costs (Cloet et al., 2024, p. 1), so the better a new crop pays the less a farm gives up on each hectare it moves to it. Quinoa, in a study for Flanders, yields about 3 tonnes a hectare, sold at €1,100 a tonne under contract on a market still very small (pp. 2–3). Within the year: the crop is chosen each season.
attributes.simplification: Draws the price as lowering the margin given up by the same amount whatever the adoption, though it acts only on the hectares already moved to new crops, not on those under tolerant varieties, which the element also counts: while few fields grow a new crop, a better price changes the total little, and while none do, nothing. The effect weakens but never reverses, so the link keeps its sign and every loop through it keeps its polarity: the shortest, a better price lifting Farm income, Farmers' capacity to invest and the harvest that draws a local plant, stays reinforcing. What one strength leaves out is that the price and the hectares moved act together.

attributes.description: Banks look more and more at a farm's cash flow, whether its operations earn enough to meet all its financial obligations (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 19): the bank judges whether the farmer can generate enough over the longer term for interest and repayment, the expected income being the limiting factor rather than the size of the farm (Farjon et al., 2013, section Financiering van bedrijfsuitbreiding). Basel IV steers banks further toward profitability and liquidity rather than the value of collateral (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 47). So the less a farm earns, the more risk its bank sees, for owner and tenant alike; for the Netherlands. Within the year.

attributes.description: Summers with less rain and more evaporation lower the year's rain surplus, which is what refills the lens, so the lens thins. The rain surplus falls mostly in winter, since in summer by far most of the moisture evaporates (van Beekom et al., 1953a, p. 155, for the Netherlands). In a model of a drained field over saline seepage, built from measurements on the island, the recharge is each day's rain minus evaporation: in the year it used, summer evaporation (440 mm) outweighed summer rain (425 mm), so the winter did the recharging, and a smaller surplus gave a thinner lens (de Louw et al., 2011, pp. 3665, 3671, 3674). Model calculations show that higher summer evaporation shrinks the lens (de Louw et al., 2015, p. 12, in an article on the island's seepage fields, by researchers who then present Drains2buffer, a drainage design developed in the GO-FRESH project, as a way to grow the lens). Years, so a delay: the lens is a Stock that a year's recharge barely moves. In a model of a drained field over saline seepage, built from measurements on the island, the centre of the mixing zone moves at most 0.1 m in a year as the recharge swings with the seasons, the vertical flow at most 1.2 mm a day, and every run settled from saline groundwater to a stationary lens within 30 years (de Louw et al., 2011, pp. 3665, 3673), so a change in recharge takes years to show in the lens.
attributes.simplification: Folds Rainwater lens recharge in the low polders, the rain that soaks in and refills the lens, between the two: Hotter, drier summers moves the recharge (-), and the recharge builds the lens over years (+). The sign is the product of the two steps, so no loop through the link changes, and the lens's slowness, which sat on the recharge -> thickness link, is this link's delay. Recharge is no actor's decision: the decisions that reach it, the farmers' storage measures and the water board's ditch levels, act on Winter rain drained away, which stays drawn, so no decision leaves the drawing. Hotter, drier summers is a Constant, so no loop runs through this link.

attributes.description: More winter rain raises the winter's rain surplus, which soaks in and refills the lens. In a model of a drained field over saline seepage, built from measurements on the island, the recharge is each day's rain minus evaporation, and from October to March of the year it used 397 mm of rain fell against 108 mm of evaporation (de Louw et al., 2011, p. 3665). Kaandorp et al. (2022, p. 11) expect the changing rain to raise the island's winter groundwater levels in part. The drains cap how much of a wetter winter reaches the lens: model calculations show that the extra winter water of wetter winters leaves through the intensive tile drainage and does not feed the lens (de Louw et al., 2015, p. 12, in an article on the island's seepage fields, by researchers who then present Drains2buffer, a drainage design developed in the GO-FRESH project, as a way to grow the lens); that part is drawn as Wetter winters -> Winter rain drained away. Years, so a delay: the lens is a Stock that a year's recharge barely moves. In a model of a drained field over saline seepage, built from measurements on the island, the centre of the mixing zone moves at most 0.1 m in a year as the recharge swings with the seasons, the vertical flow at most 1.2 mm a day, and every run settled from saline groundwater to a stationary lens within 30 years (de Louw et al., 2011, pp. 3665, 3673), so a change in recharge takes years to show in the lens.

Recharge is no actor's decision: the decisions that reach it, the farmers' storage measures and the water board's ditch levels, act on Winter rain drained away, which stays drawn, so no decision leaves the drawing. attributes.description: Rain refills the lens only once it has soaked into the soil. Before the floods, Zeeland's well-drained clay let the winter's rain surplus soak through almost completely; once sodium had broken down the structure of the topsoil, it became impervious and sticky when wet, part of the rain ran off over the surface and pools stood on the land, the more so the heavier the clay (van Beekom et al., 1953a, p. 157; 1953b, pp. 230, 233, 236, measured in the flooded polders of Zeeland, by R1's own mechanism). Even so, in most of the well-drained soils at least 150 mm still seeped through in winter, and less in badly drained soils of low permeability, against a Dutch annual rain surplus of about 200 mm, most of it in winter (van Beekom et al., 1953a, pp. 155, 157). In model computations of wetter winters, the extra winter water drained off effectively through the intensive drainage without feeding the thin rain lenses of the saline seepage areas the authors studied in Zeeland, among them a tile-drained field on the island, so more rain soaking in may add little to the lens (de Louw et al., 2015, pp. 6, 11, 12, by authors who report on the GO-FRESH project, which developed a drainage system to grow the lens). The structure a soil has in a winter sets how much of that winter's rain soaks in, within the year; the slowness sits in the lens. Years, so a delay: the lens is a Stock that a year's recharge barely moves. In a model of a drained field over saline seepage, built from measurements on the island, the centre of the mixing zone moves at most 0.1 m in a year as the recharge swings with the seasons, the vertical flow at most 1.2 mm a day, and every run settled from saline groundwater to a stationary lens within 30 years (de Louw et al., 2011, pp. 3665, 3673), so a change in recharge takes years to show in the lens. How thick a lens the recharge builds is also set by the drainage depth and the seepage (de Louw et al., 2011, p. 3674).
attributes.simplification: Folds Rainwater lens recharge in the low polders, the rain that soaks in and refills the lens, between the two: Soil structure moves the recharge (+), and the recharge builds the lens over years (+). The sign is the product of the two steps, so no loop through the link changes, and the lens's slowness, which sat on the recharge -> thickness link, is this link's delay. Recharge is no actor's decision: the decisions that reach it, the farmers' storage measures and the water board's ditch levels, act on Winter rain drained away, which stays drawn, so no decision leaves the drawing. R1 runs through it: Root zone salinity -(-, delay)-> Soil structure -(+, delay)-> Rainwater lens thickness -(-)-> Root zone salinity, two minus signs, reinforcing as before, and its mechanism, salty soil taking in less rain so the lens thins over years, is this link's description.

attributes.description: Rain the drains carry off does not refill the lens, so the lens thins: tile drains usually discharge shallow groundwater rapidly during rain, as other studies found (de Louw et al., 2011, p. 3661), and model calculations show that the extra winter water leaves through the intensive tile drainage and does not feed the lens (de Louw et al., 2015, p. 12). On Schouwen-Duiveland upward saline seepage keeps the recharge within the clay and peat top layer of the low polders (de Louw et al., 2011, pp. 3662, 3674–3675), and recharge, seepage and drainage depth together set the lens's thickness, by measurements on the island and a model built from them (pp. 3662, 3673–3675). In a conceptual 2-D model of a tile-drained field with saline seepage, built from field measurements in Zeeland and a 3-D model of a field on the island, how readily the drains run (a drainage resistance of 0.5 to 7.5 days) changed the lens's depth and width by less than 0.1 m; across the model's parameters the lens's depth moved more between the drains than at them, where the centre of the mixing zone stayed within 0.1 m of drain depth (de Louw et al., 2011, pp. 3662, 3664–3666, 3671). The rain drained away follows each rain within the year; the slowness sits in the lens. Years, so a delay: the lens is a Stock that a year's recharge barely moves. In a model of a drained field over saline seepage, built from measurements on the island, the centre of the mixing zone moves at most 0.1 m in a year as the recharge swings with the seasons, the vertical flow at most 1.2 mm a day, and every run settled from saline groundwater to a stationary lens within 30 years (de Louw et al., 2011, pp. 3665, 3673), so a change in recharge takes years to show in the lens. The drains cap how much of a wetter winter reaches the lens: model calculations show that the extra winter water of wetter winters leaves through the intensive tile drainage and does not feed the lens (de Louw et al., 2015, p. 12, in an article on the island's seepage fields, by researchers who then present Drains2buffer, a drainage design developed in the GO-FRESH project, as a way to grow the lens).
attributes.simplification: Folds Rainwater lens recharge in the low polders, the rain that soaks in and refills the lens, between the two: Winter rain drained away moves the recharge (-), and the recharge builds the lens over years (+). The sign is the product of the two steps, so no loop through the link changes, and the lens's slowness, which sat on the recharge -> thickness link, is this link's delay. Recharge is no actor's decision: the decisions that reach it, the farmers' storage measures and the water board's ditch levels, act on Winter rain drained away, which stays drawn, so no decision leaves the drawing. B6 and R4 run through it, with every other loop through the chain: Freshwater storage measures -(-)-> Winter rain drained away -(-, delay)-> Rainwater lens thickness keeps the farmers' storage acting on the lens by the rain kept in the field, B6 balancing and R4 reinforcing as before. It carries the drains' effect on the lens only through the rain they carry off. In de Louw et al.'s (2011, pp. 3664–3665) conceptual 2-D model of a tile-drained field, built from the island's field data, the depth of the tile drains also sets the lens's base (p. 3671, Fig. 12d). At a drain, the centre of the mixing zone stays within 0.1 m of the drain depth. Deeper drains give a deeper mixing zone, at and between the drains, so a thicker lens (pp. 3671, 3674, Fig. 12d). At the field's centre, the ditch's water level moved the lens by no more than 0.1 m (pp. 3665, 3671; Table 2 on p. 3666). So Polder drainage depth, the ditch level, needs no link of its own to the lens. The farms' drains are no variable. The measures that change them, controlled and anti-salinisation drainage, are counted in Freshwater storage measures, which keep the thin rainwater lens against salt (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 29). That is the sign the drawn path through Winter rain drained away gives, so B6 and R4 keep their polarity.

attributes.description: The deeper the ditch levels lie below the fields, the more peat lies above the groundwater, where it compacts and oxidises, so the land surface falls faster relative to NAP: by the water board's rules for its whole area, peat soil above the groundwater subsides in response to drainage, and where the soil is prone to settling the board changes levels with restraint to limit it (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, p. 13). The island's low polders lie on peat: in Schouwen's low polder salt-marsh soils alternate with basin clay with peat (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021b, p. 23), and under Duiveland a peat layer lies almost everywhere at −1.6 to −3.4 m NAP, under calcareous sand or light clay (2021a, p. 20), often within a metre of the surface in its low south and middle (p. 19); drained by ditches, the polders have sunk over several hundred years as the peat compacted and the clay ripened (2021b, pp. 20, 22; 2021a, p. 18). On the island the board holds Schouwen's summer levels high on purpose to limit subsidence by peat compaction, which leaves the salt-marsh soils between too little drainage depth (2021b, p. 45), and changes a level in soil prone to settling by no more than the land has subsided since (p. 50); Duiveland's plan changed levels with great care where peat lies below (2021a, p. 67). The rate of the fall follows the drainage within the year (the board weighs the risk by the summer groundwater level against the ditch level and the depth of the peat, 2021b, p. 50); the delay sits in the elevation, which the fall lowers at millimetres a year, so a decimetre takes decades: Dutch land below sea level is still subsiding up to 1 m per century, fastest in peat areas (Oude Essink et al., 2010, pp. 1, 3, 8–9). No source read gives how much faster the land falls per decimetre of drainage, nor a rate for Schouwen-Duiveland's clay polders.
attributes.simplification: Folds Land subsidence, the rate at which the polders' surface falls, into the link: the sign is the product of the two steps (+, then −), so no loop through the link changes R or B, and each keeps its mechanism, drained peat compacting and oxidising and the land falling. The rate follows the drainage within the year and is no actor's decision; its slowness lies in the elevation, a Stock, which stays drawn, so the delay sits on this link. The link also holds the rate's response to the drainage as if the peat above the groundwater lasted to 2050: its organic matter oxidises as it is drained, which uses it up, but no source read gives how much peat is left on the island or how long it lasts. Drawn, the dwindling peat would only weaken the link, in a balancing loop of its own, never reverse it, so every loop through it keeps its polarity and its mechanism. The link also counts the drainage depth and the fall of the land as totals for the island, though how fast drainage makes the land fall differs by area with where peat lies above the groundwater: in Schouwen's low polder salt-marsh soils alternate with basin clay with peat (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021b, p. 23), and under Duiveland the peat lies often within a metre of the surface in its low south and middle (2021a, p. 19), so one level does not suit every soil: on Schouwen the board holds the summer levels high for the peat, which leaves the salt-marsh soils between too little drainage depth (2021b, p. 45). Deeper drainage lowers the land wherever it acts, so the link stays − and every loop through it keeps its polarity, and those loops run on through the seepage of the low polders, where the peat lies, so they keep their mechanism. What it leaves out: how strong the link is per area, which no source read gives for the island.
attributes.ask actors: Waterschap Scheldestromen, through DCC or Living Lab: How fast the island's polders subside, per area: the board changes a level in soil prone to settling by no more than the land has subsided since (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021b, p. 50).

attributes.description: More hectares of new crops on the island give more harvest within reach of a processor or trader on or near the island, and that volume draws capacity. Quinoa has been grown in Zeeland since 2016, on one to four parcels a year at six locations in all (Bogers et al., 2025, pp. 28, 38), its map showing one of them on the island. Quinoa yields about 2,000 kg a hectare on average in Europe (van Loo, 2023, p. 79), and its yield varies from under 500 to over 4,000 kg (p. 76), harvested in the Netherlands in August of the year it is sown (p. 75). More harvest within reach makes a plant or chain nearby more worthwhile, so buyers and processors build or keep capacity on or near the island rather than handle the crops elsewhere. In France, the firms that store, process and sell crops specialised in a few dominant ones for economies of scale, and their logistics are not adapted to sorting pulses out of mixed crops (Magrini et al., 2018, pp. 3, 9), and a small volume spread out or far from its users costs more to collect and to source (Meynard et al., 2018, pp. 7–8): the economies of scale hold wherever a chain is built, so the mechanism transfers. In the Netherlands, on Terschelling's saline field, producers of processed products are more concerned about volumes than the restaurants are, and stakeholders describe a chicken and egg: a producer needs a market, and a reliable market needs ample supply (ten Dam et al., 2023, pp. 10, 14); for quinoa, one expert says efforts only work with concentrated investments and high volumes (de Wit et al., 2022, p. 270). Years: a Zeeland quinoa chain was a project from 2021 to 2024 (De Vriend, 2024a): the delay sits in building the chain, not in the harvest, which follows within the year.
attributes.simplification: Folds Harvest of new crops to process, the volume of new crops harvested in a year within reach of a processor or trader on or near the island, from the island's growers and from growers elsewhere, and before it Attractiveness of processing new crops locally: the harvest is now the step in words between the hectares (or the growers elsewhere) and the capacity they draw. It was an auxiliary no actor decides, with one link out; both steps into it are + and its link out is +, so each folded link is + and keeps the delay of building the chain. R7 runs Adoption of new crops (+, delay) Local processing capacity for new crops (+) Net price for new crops after transport (+) Adoption: reinforcing as before, on the same mechanism, volume within reach drawing a chain nearby that cuts transport; every other loop through the harvest runs through this link too and keeps its sign. The harvest within reach counts every new crop as one volume, although its crops go to separate chains: quinoa to buyers such as GreenFood50 (DutchNews.nl, 2026), samphire to a Zeeland trader in sea vegetables (FreshPlaza, 2018); read per crop, the loops run the same way, and what this leaves out is that the volume a chain needs is reached crop by crop; summed, the link overstates how soon several small crops together make a plant worthwhile.

attributes.description: A plant draws its harvest from every grower within reach, on the island or off it, so growers elsewhere add to the volume that draws capacity near the island: GreenFood50 has its quinoa grown in the Netherlands and Belgium, close to its processing facilities, to cut transport (GreenFood50, n.d.), by its growers, most of the Dutch ones, working about 200 hectares for 600 tonnes a year (DutchNews.nl, 2026). More harvest within reach makes a plant or chain nearby more worthwhile, so buyers and processors build or keep capacity on or near the island rather than handle the crops elsewhere. In France, the firms that store, process and sell crops specialised in a few dominant ones for economies of scale, and their logistics are not adapted to sorting pulses out of mixed crops (Magrini et al., 2018, pp. 3, 9), and a small volume spread out or far from its users costs more to collect and to source (Meynard et al., 2018, pp. 7–8): the economies of scale hold wherever a chain is built, so the mechanism transfers. In the Netherlands, on Terschelling's saline field, producers of processed products are more concerned about volumes than the restaurants are, and stakeholders describe a chicken and egg: a producer needs a market, and a reliable market needs ample supply (ten Dam et al., 2023, pp. 10, 14); for quinoa, one expert says efforts only work with concentrated investments and high volumes (de Wit et al., 2022, p. 270). Years: a Zeeland quinoa chain was a project from 2021 to 2024 (De Vriend, 2024a): the delay sits in building the chain, not in the harvest, which follows within the year.
attributes.simplification: Folds Harvest of new crops to process, the volume of new crops harvested in a year within reach of a processor or trader on or near the island, from the island's growers and from growers elsewhere, and before it Attractiveness of processing new crops locally: the harvest is now the step in words between the growers elsewhere and the capacity they draw. Both steps are +, so the link is + and keeps the delay of building the chain; no loop runs through it, since Growers of new crops elsewhere is a constant. What it adds to Local processing capacity for new crops is the off-island part of the volume within reach, which the link from Adoption of new crops adds the island's part to; counted as one volume over crops, although quinoa and samphire go to separate chains (DutchNews.nl, 2026; FreshPlaza, 2018). It also treats the growers of new crops off the island as fixed, while GreenFood50 has its quinoa grown close to its processing facilities, to cut transport (GreenFood50, n.d.), so a plant on or near the island could also draw growers from nearby off the island. That response would close a loop of two links, from Local processing capacity for new crops back to Growers of new crops elsewhere and through this link back to the capacity, with no minus sign, reinforcing beside R7, so leaving it out changes no drawn loop's polarity or mechanism; what it leaves out is how much of a nearby plant's harvest would come from growers off the island rather than the island's own.

attributes.description: Each hectare moved adds to the hectares under new crops, where it stays while the farm grows the crop: the switch is the Stock's yearly inflow, a farmers' measure that van Duinen et al. (2015a, p. 1085) list among those for drought in the south-west Netherlands. Within the year.

attributes.description: The more salt or brackish seepage wells up, the saltier the ditches that catch it: in most of Duiveland the ditches catch the salt or brackish seepage from below (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, p. 20), and in the low polders of the island's west, where salt groundwater lies at a small depth, the surface water is brackish to salt (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 27). Within the season.

attributes.description: In a dry period less rain drains into the ditches to dilute their salt: in one area studied on the island, there were indications that the main ditches were less brackish after periods of rain, as drained rain mixed in, and in dry periods their salt seemed partly to come from salt surface water brought in from elsewhere (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 42). Measured in one area of the island. Within the season.

attributes.description: Salt ditch water cannot fill a measure that infiltrates water: in one area studied on the island the main ditches are expected to carry water all year, but in general brackish to salt and with iron and turbidity that can clog wells, so in the current situation it is unsuited for infiltration into the deeper subsoil (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 43), and the fresh water infiltration needs is a bottleneck at most of the island's locations, which, beside the rules, limits the large-scale roll-out of the infiltration solutions (p. 55). So it limits how far the measures that infiltrate spread, not what one measure delivers. No delay drawn: no source read gives how fast the roll-out answers the salt.

attributes.description: The more of the rotation is under potatoes and onions, the more water the crop plan needs: on the island the crops that earn the most also have the greatest water need and often a limited root system (Delphy, 2023, p. 48). Within the year, as the rotation is set.

attributes.description: The shortfall is what crops need beyond the water they get, so with the water available unchanged a crop plan that needs more water leaves a larger gap: a crop's need is the water it uses when it has enough (Allen et al., 1998). On the island the farms' total need is put at about 3.5 million m³ (Delphy, 2023, p. 41), and the total need of all its sectors goes beyond what the current sources give (p. 50). Within the season.

attributes.description: A farm short of water moves off the crops that need it most: in a low-polder area studied on the island, the farmer would be open to more profitable crops, a more varied rotation, or both, with more fresh water (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 30). On the island the sown onions fell from 1,214 ha in 2015 to 791 ha in 2022 (Delphy, 2023, p. 15), and without fresh water they leave the model farm's crop plan for 2030 (p. 44); in Zeeland they halved from 4,705 ha in 2019 to 2,579 ha in 2024, the article naming the dry summers, the poor harvests and the lack of fresh water, four in five arable farmers having none, as farmers preferred less risky crops (De Vriend, 2024b, for Zeeland). Years, so a delay: farmers respond to the seasons they have had, and the fall ran over five years of dry summers.
attributes.simplification: Folds Farmers' experience of damage, a stock that builds over dry summers, into this link's delay: farmers respond to the damage they come to notice, not to the state of the soil. Every loop through the link keeps its polarity and its mechanism, and the delay is kept; what it leaves out is how far what farmers notice differs from what the soil shows.

attributes.description: Trials and pilots give farmers and advisers what a measure does on the island: the quickscans and feasibility studies of Samenwerken voor Zoet Water made methods, maps and tools with which farmers and advisers can go on by themselves (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 55), and its authors recommend pilots with monitoring, since farmers are sooner willing to invest in a solution whose working has been shown in practice somewhere (p. 56); the demonstration on three farms monitored new drainage for figures and guidelines on building, managing and maintaining it (Living Lab Schouwen-Duiveland, n.d.-b). Years, so a delay: many studies have started or are running, and a picture of their result comes only after years (Delphy, 2023, p. 40).

Measured in Zeeland: no source read shows a trial raising what the island's own farmers know. Years, so a delay, as for the water measures, whose results show only after years (p. 40).

attributes.description: The more firmly a supply route is asked for, the more farmers hold back from storing on their own farm: on the island some parties hold that the answer to drought damage lies either in a supply from outside or in local measures, and through this ongoing discussion farmers hold back from investing, while the one need not exclude the other and can strengthen it (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 12). No route is decided: a study of the options leaves who pays what, and how a supply would be managed, for later steps (Witteveen+Bos, 2021, p. 51). The branch also asks to catch more rain, beside a collective supply (Omroep Zeeland, 2023). No delay drawn: no source read gives how fast the farmers' hesitation follows the call.

attributes.description: The more a farmer expects to lose on a new crop, the fewer fields move to it. On the island the cost of unproven innovations lies mainly with the farmer, so investing carries a risk (Delphy, 2023, p. 50); in the south-west Netherlands, farmers who saw a higher cost in drought measures took fewer of them (van Duinen et al., 2015a, p. 1089). Measured for the island's water measures and for drought measures in the south-west, not for a crop switch: that it holds for a switch too is an assumption. Within the year.

attributes.description: Do farmers who know how to grow and sell a new crop see less risk in switching to it? A hypothesis for the group model building session: no source read measures the risk farmers see in a new crop against what they know of it, so the question to farmers is whether knowing a crop lowers the risk they see in it. Within the year, if it holds.

The more demand for a new crop, the more of it buyers contract: Dutch quinoa's one distributor buys a pre-agreed amount and manages supply according to demand (de Wit et al., 2022, pp. 266, 268), and for saline crops in Zeeland sales would have to grow strongly before new growers find room (Delphy, 2023, p. 49). Measured in the Netherlands and in Zeeland. Within the year.

attributes.description: A contract takes the price and sales risk of a crop off the farmer as far as its terms go, as Dutch potato contracts show: a fixed-price contract guarantees the price for the agreed quantity and a volume contract the sale, provided the crop meets the agreed quality, the contracted part carrying an offtake duty (Janssens et al., 2020, pp. 11–12), while a grower who sells free bears a loss alone (p. 15); it moves no yield risk. Measured for potatoes nationally. With one buyer the farmer keeps that buyer's risk: Dutch quinoa growers depend on one distributor, which interviewees name as hampering its uptake (de Wit et al., 2022, p. 268). Within the year.

attributes.description: A farm without a successor stops sooner: on the island, Delphy expects farms caught in a downward spiral to decide, without a successor, to stop, with more scale and more extensive farming following (Delphy, 2023, p. 50), and since 2000 the island's arable area fell 21% while its grassland and forage crops grew 52% (p. 14). Nationally, farms end mainly at the change of generation, the lack of a successor among the reasons, while the land's buyers and sellers are mainly farmers (Silvis & Voskuilen, 2017, p. 2), so most land of a farm that stops stays arable: the link is weak, and no source read gives how much of a stopped farm's land leaves arable farming on the island. Within the year the farm stops.

attributes.description: Does a farm short of water move fields to a new crop that copes with little water, as one losing harvest to salt moves them to a crop that copes with salt (Harvest lost to salt → Fields moved to new crops)? A hypothesis for the group model building session: under drought, the response a source shows on the island is to a crop the farms already grow, cereals (Crop water shortfall → Dependence on high-margin salt-sensitive crops), so the question to farmers is whether a shortfall moves them to a new crop at all, and to which. Years, if it holds, as farms respond to the dry seasons they have had, as in that link, along which the island's sown onions fell from 2015 to 2022: a delay.

The larger the share of the rotation under the crops salt harms most, the more of the harvest salt takes at the same root zone salinity: onions lose 16% of their yield per dS/m above 1.2 dS/m and potatoes 12% above 1.7, against 5.9% above 7.0 for sugar beet and 7.1% above 6.0 for wheat (Allen et al., 1998, ch. 8, Table 23), lines that give the sign on the island but not the size of the loss (Root zone salinity → Harvest lost to salt). On the island, farms where the seepage pressure is high and the surface water salty all year have stopped growing sensitive crops such as sown onions (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 31), which lowers what salt can take. The link counts the shift among the current crops; a field moved to a new crop leaves the loss by Adoption of new crops → Harvest lost to salt. Within the season.
attributes.sources:

Deltares. https://livinglabschouwen-duiveland.nl/sites/default/files/2022-07/112059~1.PDF

attributes.description: The crops that stand salt the least are the ones that earn the most: potatoes are financially attractive, the most important crop of Dutch arable farming (Verhagen et al., 2018, p. 12), and on specialised arable farms on clay growing ware potatoes they bring in, on average over the years, 55% of the arable revenue, against 14% for onions and 11% for sugar beet (Janssens et al., 2020, p. 14); in Zeeland, a manager of the cooperative CZAV says, a farmer earns his money not with rotation crops but with onions, beets and potatoes (Economic Board Zeeland, 2023, p. 19). So a farm that keeps more of them earns more in a year, less what salt takes, which Dependence on high-margin salt-sensitive crops → Harvest lost to salt counts. No source read sizes the net effect of the crop mix on the island's incomes. Within the year.
attributes.sources:
Verhagen, J., van Asseldonk, M., & Pronk, A. A. (2018). Open teelten en klimaatadaptatie in relatie tot de financiële weerbaarheid (Rapport WPR-755). attributes.description: Does a salt-tolerant variety of potato or onion let a farm keep those crops on a field that salt would otherwise take them off? A hypothesis for the group model building session: a tolerant variety uses the same machines, storage and know-how as the variety it replaces (Adoption of salt-tolerant varieties), but no source read shows one grown on the island, nor a farm keeping its potatoes because of one, so the question to farmers is whether a tolerant variety would make them keep those crops. Within the year, if it holds.

The more the water falls short of what crops need, the more worthwhile farmers find storing it, and those who can pay for it store more. On the island the attention to drought and to waterlogging swings with dry and wet years, and the study names this swinging urgency among the barriers to scaling up storage (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 12): a dry year raises the push to store, a wet one lets it fade. In the island's western low polders, farmers find the winter's rain surplus enough to prevent the drought damage, holding or storing it being the limiting factor (p. 27). The shortfall is the gap farmers' water decisions respond to, as for pumping and the call for a supply route. No delay drawn: how quickly a dry summer turns into a measure built, no source read shows.
attributes.simplification: Folds Relative attractiveness of storing water, which gathered the drivers of this decision: each driver now points at Freshwater storage measures itself, whose description says how farmers weigh storing against their other ways through a dry summer. The shortfall raised the attractiveness and the attractiveness the decision, so the link keeps the sign of the steps it folds and no loop through it changes; the attractiveness was no actor's decision of its own. What it leaves out: whether farmers want to store, apart from whether they can (Farmers' capacity to invest), is no variable on the drawing, only in the description.
attributes.sources: Kaandorp, V. P., Davids, T., de Louw, P. G. B., Roelandse, A., Noordegraaf, I., Krajenbrink, H. J., Schout, G., Raat, K. J., & van Veelen, P. C. (2022). Samenwerken voor zoet water Schouwen-Duiveland – van pilots naar grootschalige toepassing: Eindrapport (11205909-000-BGS-0003). Deltares. https://livinglabschouwen-duiveland.nl/sites/default/files/2022-07/112059~1.PDF

attributes.description: Does the harvest salt takes make farmers store more fresh water in their fields? In the low polders the measures keep the thin rainwater lens against salt (Freshwater storage measures), so a farm losing harvest to salt has a reason to take them up beside the shortfall. A hypothesis for the group model building session: no source read shows a farmer storing because of salt damage, so the question to farmers is whether salt on their fields makes them consider such measures. No delay drawn: how quickly salt damage turns into a measure built, no source read shows.

A new loan adds to what a farm owes until its repayments, the periodic amounts that pay it back within the agreed term, have paid it off (ABN AMRO, n.d.-a). Refinancing replaces a loan and adds no debt, so the link counts the new money, as Bank credit to farms does. Less credit slows the debt's rise; the debt itself falls through repayments (Repayments on farm loans → Farm debt). Within the year: a loan is owed once it is paid out.
attributes.sources: ABN AMRO. (n.d.-a). Kosten van een krediet. Retrieved November 7, 2026, from https://www.abnamro.nl/nl/zakelijk/producten/financieren/informatie/kosten-krediet/index.html

attributes.description: With the same assets, more debt is a higher debt relative to them and a lower solvency, solvency being its equity as a percentage of its total capital minus deferred tax (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 19). Farms that expanded in recent years have a lower solvency (Silvis & Voskuilen, 2017, p. 3); Dutch farmers under 45 had 68% in 2018 against 76% for those over 65, their higher long-term debt going partly with taking over the farm (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 26); on dairy farms heavy investment and poor results together took five points off solvency between 2006 and 2015 (Silvis et al., 2017, p. 2). The sign holds with the assets' value unchanged: the debt of Dutch arable farms rose 38% between 2010 and 2022, yet in 2022 it was 28% of their balance sheet, the smallest share in farming, as equity grows mainly through the rising value of the land (CBS, 2024). Within the year: a loan is on the balance sheet once it is paid out.

attributes.description: The more a farm owes, the more interest and commission it pays a year: they are the price of its loans, the repayment paid beside them (ABN AMRO, n.d.-a), so a loan adds to the interest each year for as long as it is owed, not only in the year it is made. Within the year: interest falls due from the loan's payout.

attributes.description: The margin given up is net of what the tolerant variety earns, a margin being revenue minus the crop's variable costs (Cloet et al., 2024, p. 1), so the better the tolerant varieties on offer yield, the less a farm gives up on each hectare it moves to one. Tolerant varieties yield relatively little against common high-yielding ones without salt or under mild salt (van den Burg et al., 2024, p. 6), high-yielding varieties being sensitive to stress through a trade-off between tolerance and yield (Deolu-Ajayi et al., 2024, p. 30); in greenhouse pots at Wageningen in 2024, a salt-tolerant potato variety netted about €1,800 a hectare on fresh water with the soil amendment that served it best, against about €2,300 for the sensitive, high-yielding variety grown as usual (pp. 51–52). Within the season: the variety is chosen each season.
attributes.simplification: Draws the yield as lowering the margin given up by the same amount whatever the adoption, though it acts only on the hectares already under a tolerant variety, not on those moved to new crops, which the element also counts: while few fields grow a tolerant variety, a better yield changes the total little, and while none do, nothing. The effect weakens but never reverses, so the link keeps its sign, and it closes no loop, since the varieties on offer have no links in. What one strength leaves out is that the yield and the hectares under tolerant varieties act together.

attributes.description: A farm short of cash first cuts maintenance and private spending or draws on its savings, and if that is not enough can ask its bank to defer part of its interest and repayments or for more credit (Verhagen et al., 2018, p. 28), so the less a farm has of its own to spend, the more credit it asks for, the bank weighing the request (Banks' risk assessment of farm loans → Bank credit to farms). The source describes credit asked to bridge a cash shortfall; no source read shows how the island's farms borrow to invest. Farmers also hold back: Rabobank's outstanding agricultural loans fell between 2010 and 2018 largely because farmers asked for less credit amid uncertainty over future environmental and climate rules (Banken.nl, 2019, for the Netherlands as a whole and all farm types), a driver no variable carries. Why the island's farmers ask or hold back is a question for the group model building session. Within the year: a farm asks when it runs short.

attributes.description: The larger the share of a loan to be repaid each year, the more a farm pays its banks a year on the same debt: the repayment pays a loan back within the agreed term (ABN AMRO, n.d.-a), so a shorter term raises it, as ABN AMRO's cut from fifty to forty years on new farmland financing did, to at least 2.5% a year (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 47).
