attributes.label: R1 Salty soil takes in less rain
attributes.description: Salt in the root zone puts sodium on the clay; once fresh water washes the salt out, the soil's structure collapses and recovers only over years. Less rain soaks in, less recharges the rainwater lens, the lens thins over years and saline groundwater comes closer to the roots: more salt. It runs in the low polders. The mechanism was measured after seawater floods; how much sodium the island's seepage puts on its clay, no source read shows. R1 may be weak on tile-drained fields such as the one measured on the island: in model computations extra winter water leaves through the intensive drainage without feeding the lens (de Louw et al., 2015, pp. 11, 12), and after a seawater flood most well-drained soils still let at least 150 mm through in winter (van Beekom et al., 1953a, p. 157). No practice is on it: the salt it adds drives tolerant crops and varieties (B2, B1).

attributes.label: B1 Salt losses move fields to tolerant varieties
attributes.description: The more harvest salt takes, the more a tolerant variety is worth against the one grown now, so after the dry summers that bring the damage to notice, and perhaps only past a threshold, more farmers grow it. A tolerant variety loses less to salt, so the harvest lost falls. It seeks the loss at which a farmer changes variety, a hypothesis for the group model building session: unlike the move to new crops (B2), no source shows that salt losses move farmers to another variety. Tolerant varieties use the same machines, storage and know-how, so little capital is lost on them (R3). It drives tolerant varieties.

attributes.label: B2 Salt losses move fields to new crops
attributes.description: The more harvest salt takes, the more a new crop that copes with salt is worth against the current crops, so after the dry summers that bring the damage to notice, and perhaps only past a threshold, more farmers grow it. A field moved no longer has a conventional harvest for salt to take, so the harvest lost falls; the salt stays in the soil. It seeks the loss at which a farmer switches: that farmers hold back until salt severely hits their production rests on sources, what sets each farmer's threshold, through their crops, margins, buyers and bank, is a hypothesis for the group model building session. On the island no source read shows B2 at work: the shift its farmers show is from onions to cereals, a crop they already grow and no new one, which the source puts down to drought (Raat et al., 2026, p. 49). With B1 and B3 it is a way out of the same salt: switching keeps the land arable, B3 is arable farming ending. It drives new crops.

attributes.label: B3 Land leaving arable use lets levels rise and salt fall
attributes.description: More salt in the root zone takes more of the harvest, income and land value fall, and where arable farming no longer pays for a buyer or successor the land goes to a holder who does not farm it as arable land. With less arable land the water board, whose level follows the land's use, has more reason to raise the ditch levels, over years; seepage falls, the rainwater lens thickens and the salt falls back. It seeks the salt level at which arable farming stops paying for any successor or buyer, set by crop prices, margins and the land market. With B2 and B1 it is a way out of the same salt: those keep the land arable with another crop, this one is arable farming ending, where the current crops stop paying and adapting does not pay or is not chosen. It acts only at that end: while arable farming still pays for someone, land from a farm that stops mostly goes to expanding neighbours and stays arable (Arable land in the polders), and a raise follows only where a whole level area leaves arable use, since where nature and farmland share one on Duiveland the plan keeps nature's level and keeps the farm parcel draining (Arable land in the polders → Water board's plans to raise ditch levels). On Duiveland most raises wait for more discharge capacity, and the province's norm for storage and discharge holds for grassland as for arable land (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, pp. 12, 33–34, 69), so, by inference, a level area that goes from arable crops to grass would mostly still wait for the discharge works, and the loop is weaker still there. From salt to a raise takes decades, its slowest steps the land changing hands and the board's plan cycle.

attributes.label: B4 Deep drainage keeps fields workable
attributes.description: Where fields stay too wet to work in spring, farmers ask for low ditch levels and the water board plans fewer raises. The levels stay low, the fields drain and dry sooner, and the wish for lower levels eases. On Duiveland it has room mainly in the 10 of 31 level areas with more than 10% of their surface too wet in a normal winter, since in large parts of the area the drooglegging already exceeds its optimum by more than 40 cm (60 cm on schorgronden) (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, pp. 32, 42). It seeks fields dry enough for heavy machinery in spring: what deep drainage gains a farm, R2 tracing what it costs. By keeping the current crops' spring work possible, it supports carrying on with them rather than adopting a practice.

attributes.label: R2 Debt and deep drainage feed each other through salt
attributes.description: A farm with higher leverage is a riskier loan, so banks charge a higher premium and its debt payments rise. To meet them it keeps its high-margin, salt-sensitive crops, whose spring soil work needs fields that dry early, so farmers ask for low ditch levels and the water board, weighing that against raising them, plans fewer raises. The levels stay low, saline seepage stays higher, the rainwater lens thins over years, salt takes more of the harvest, income and land value fall, and leverage rises. It closes only through a hypothesis, Debt payments → Dependence on high-margin salt-sensitive crops, which no source read tests; where indebted farms choose less risky crops instead, the loop breaks there. It shows an unintended consequence of the deep drainage in B4: the gain comes within the season, the seepage and salt years later. It holds back new crops through the dependence it keeps up, while the salt it adds pushes towards them (B2, B1).

attributes.label: R3 Capital ties farms to their crops
attributes.description: A farm tied to its current crops spends on keeping them as machines and stores fall due, over years. The more it owns for those crops, the more a switch to a new crop would write off, and what it would lose ties it further to them. It holds back new crops, and leaves tolerant varieties of the current crops nearly untouched. On Schouwen-Duiveland R3 may be weak: its farm-level evidence is a store built in the Limburg loess and one farmer's plans for water storage, while the island's own farmer ties the low cost of a less intensive rotation there to the lack of fresh water, and the workshop and an exploration of the island tie the share of sensitive crops to it and to drought (Dijkshoorn-Dekker et al., 2024, pp. 56–57, 59, 71; Raat et al., 2026, pp. 34, 49).

attributes.label: B5 Pumping relieves the shortfall
attributes.description: As the crop water shortfall grows, farmers pump more fresh groundwater, crops get more water and the shortfall shrinks, within the season. It seeks the water the crop needs, and runs only where a farm has fresh groundwater more than 15 m thick under it, on the creek ridges and dunes; the farmers talked to in the low polders do not irrigate. Across the whole island it can move little: groundwater irrigation, taken at the permitted maximum, a figure the authors call probably inaccurate, is about one hundredth of the 2018 precipitation deficit (Krajenbrink et al., 2023, pp. 44–46, 48). Where it eases the shortfall it eases the worse harvests that make storing worthwhile (B6), so it can hold storage back.

attributes.label: B6 Farms store water when water falls short
attributes.description: As the water falls short of what crops need, farmers find storing it more worthwhile and those who can pay for it store more. Less winter rain drains away, the rainwater lens thickens over years, crops on that field have more fresh water and the shortfall shrinks. It seeks the shortfall at which storing stops being worth its cost, which each farmer sets against their other ways through a dry summer. On the island's two trials of the lens-growing measures the lens's growth was not clearly shown: at Kerkwerve freshening was measured at 3 of 5 locations and the effect 'lijkt daarmee beperkt' (Oude Essink et al., 2018, p. 97), and near Dreischor its growth was '(nog) niet aangetoond' over the measuring period, perhaps because of height differences within the plot or because the fresh-salt system responds slowly (van Hateren et al., 2025, p. 59). It drives storage, slowly, the lens taking years to respond.

attributes.label: B7 A shortfall brings calls for a supply route
attributes.description: The shorter of water the farms, the more firmly Agrarisch Schouwen-Duiveland asks for a supply route, and the deciding body weighs that call over the years a route takes to decide, pay for and build. A route would carry fresh water to the island, crops would have more to draw on and the shortfall would shrink. A route drawing on the Volkerak-Zoommeer would ease the shortfall little late in the season, when algae closed such inlets on Tholen in most years 2003–2011 (Schipper et al., 2014, p. 36); the Haringvliet source with a ring pipeline gives the best water but the highest costs (Witteveen+Bos, 2021, p. 50). None exists, so the loop has not run yet; a study has left open who pays and who would run one. It seeks a shortfall the deciding body finds acceptable. Where it eased the shortfall it would ease the worse harvests that make storing worthwhile (B6).

attributes.label: B8 Pumping rules protect the lens
attributes.description: Under the creek ridges and dunes, the thicker the fresh groundwater, the more pumping the water board's rules allow. Farmers pump within that, and what they pump beyond what the rain puts back thins the lens. It seeks the balance between recharge and extraction on which the board set its limit. On the island the rules answer the lens at the 15 m threshold, not along it: a lens that thins while still at 15 m or more keeps the same 800 m³ per hectare (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2026f, arts. 1.1 and 2.9), and after a map revision leaves wells outside the fresh bodies, those in use may still be used and only new ones are refused (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2019, p. 20). It shows an unintended consequence of the pumping in B5: a thinner lens, which reaches crops only through wells, so it comes back only through what the rules allow. For storage on the creek ridges, what infiltration adds to this lens is what wells can pump.

attributes.label: R4 Storage keeps up the income that pays for it
attributes.description: A farm with more left to invest can pay for more storage measures, so less winter rain drains away, more recharges the rainwater lens, the lens thickens over years, crops on that field have more fresh water, the shortfall shrinks, and yield, income and what the farm can invest rise. Run backwards, a farm with little left to invest cannot pay for storage, its water gets scarcer and its income falls further: the financial pressure R2 traces through what farms do, R4 traces through what they cannot do. It runs in the low polders. It drives storage on farms with the means and holds it back on farms without.

attributes.label: R5 Storing teaches how storage works
attributes.description: The more measures are built and monitored on the island, the more its farmers, advisers and contractors know of how storage works there and what it costs, risks and yields, and the readier farmers are to invest. Run backwards, where farms do not invest nothing is learned and no knowledge base forms. It drives storage once measures are built and holds it back while few are. It reinforces where what is learned shows a measure works on the farm's ground, and not where it shows the ground unsuited: at Kerkwerve, on the island, monitoring found the effect of anti-salinisation drainage seems limited on unripened clay with a high ditch level and old shallow drains left largely working (Oude Essink et al., 2018, p. 97). How long this takes, no source read shows.

attributes.label: R6 Falling land value cuts the credit to switch
attributes.description: When farmland loses value, the same mortgage is more debt against the farm's assets, so banks see more risk and lend less. The farm has less to invest and moves fewer fields to new crops, more of its conventional harvest stays exposed to salt, income falls and the land loses more value. It runs for farms that own their land. Dutch arable farms' solvency was generally high, 81% in 2018, owing to rising land values (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 21), against the 30% Dutch banks in general require (fi-compass, 2020, p. 26), so on many island farms a fall in land value may cut credit little. It shows an unintended consequence of the banks' response in B9: a bank limits its lending to protect itself, and farms that get less credit adapt less, which lowers the collateral further. It holds back new crops where land loses value and supports them where land keeps it.

attributes.label: B9 Banks lend less as leverage rises
attributes.description: A farm with higher leverage is a riskier loan, so banks lend it less, less new debt is added and its leverage stops rising. It seeks the leverage a bank accepts, and is the banks' intended loop: they limit their exposure. By limiting credit it holds back what a farm can invest in new crops and storage; R6 shows what that can do in turn.

attributes.label: B10 Switching gives up margin
attributes.description: Moving a field to a new crop gives up the current crop's margin, most on fresh land where the current crops still do well. Income and land value fall, leverage and the bank's risk rise, credit falls and the farm has less to invest, so fewer fields move. It seeks the share of new crops that a farm's income and credit can carry. It shares its chain with R6, where the switch saves harvest instead; a sign cannot say which pulls harder, so that is a question for the group. It holds back new crops.

attributes.label: R7 Growers draw a plant, and a plant draws growers
attributes.description: More hectares under new crops give more harvest within reach of a plant, which makes a local plant more worthwhile to buyers and processors. A plant nearby cuts transport, farmers keep more of the price, the crop is worth more and more farmers grow it. Run backwards, few hectares leave no reason for a plant and transport keeps the price low. It drives new crops once enough is grown and holds them back while too little is. Where a new crop is sold under contract to one buyer, as Dutch quinoa is in interviews published in 2022, that buyer purchases a pre-agreed amount and no other buyer competes (de Wit et al., 2022, pp. 266, 268), which means a nearby plant draws more growers only as fast as the demand that buyer supplies grows.

attributes.label: B11 The water board raises levels against seepage
attributes.description: Lower ditch levels raise the saline seepage. The water board names the salinisation a concern and aims to keep or enlarge the lenses, so over years more seepage gives it more reason to plan raises; once carried out, the levels rise and the seepage falls. It seeks the fresh water in the soil the board wants to keep; how far seepage weighs against drought in its plans, no source read shows. On the island the board's accounts read give the loop little support: the board raises levels on Schouwen to limit drought damage, with larger fresh water stocks in the soil as the effect (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021b, p. 53), and its 2025 framework for level plans names neither seepage nor the lenses among its criteria (2025, pp. 9, 12), so of the accounts read only the Duiveland report names the lenses among its reasons for a raise (2021a, p. 37). It touches adoption only through the salt it lowers (B2, B1).

attributes.label: B12 The board tests the drainage depth
attributes.description: The water board tests each level area's drainage depth against the optimum for its use and soil: where little of the area is too wet a raise is considered, where much of it is the target level is lowered or the discharge's bottlenecks solved. Carried out over years, the depth moves back towards that optimum, which the board sets by its own rules. It touches adoption only through the seepage and salt the ditch level sets.

attributes.label: B13 Objections hold back plans
attributes.description: A plan to raise ditch levels brings objections, appeals and lobbying from landowning farmers who expect it to lower their land's value; whether that is their reason is a question for the group model building session. Objections can delay, change or stop the plan while it is pending, so fewer raises stay planned. On the island the views changed neither 2021 level plan, as the board summarises them, not Schouwen's raise in ten level areas nor Duiveland's proposed study of a raise (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021b, pp. 8, 53; 2021a, p. 53), so no source read shows objections holding back a raise there. It is the objectors' intended loop, protecting their land, and seeks a plan they can accept. It touches adoption only through the levels it holds, and through R8 and R9.

attributes.label: R8 Falling land value brings objections that keep salt high
attributes.description: When farmland loses value, its owners may object harder to the next plan to raise ditch levels; whether they do is a hypothesis for the group model building session, the sign possibly opposite where compensation pays more than the land would fetch. Objections can hold today's level while a plan is pending, and never deepen it. Seepage stays higher, the rainwater lens stays thin, salt takes more of the harvest, income falls and the land loses more value. It shows an unintended consequence of the objections in B13: owners object to protect their land, and the levels held keep up the seepage and salt that lower its value. It touches adoption through the salt it keeps up (B2, B1).

attributes.label: R9 Changed plans erode trust
attributes.description: Objections and appeals delay, change or stop plans after public bodies have announced them. Plans changed or dropped teach farmers not to count on the next one, their trust in government falls, and farmers who trust less object more. The step from objections to trust is a hypothesis for the group model building session; the step from trust back to objections rests on sources. It reinforces where farmers' objections are passed over, or through the conflict itself; where a body takes them up, the step may turn positive and the loop balancing. It holds back storage, a long investment that a change of rules can strand, as trust falls.

attributes.label: B15 The water sets the crops
attributes.description: The more of the rotation is under the high-margin crops, the more water the crop plan needs and, with the water the island has, the larger the shortfall; over years, farms short of water move off those crops, sown onions first, and the shortfall shrinks. It seeks a crop plan the island's water can carry: the water is a limit farmers fit their crops to, as much as the salt. On the island the sown onions fell from 1,214 ha in 2015 to 791 ha in 2022 (Delphy, 2023, p. 15). It holds back the income the high-margin crops bring, so where a farm adapts this way it adapts by earning less.

maps.name: 01 CLD model
02 Actor Map
maps.description: The level at which an actor works, from global at the top to local at the bottom. Within a band, an actor's position says nothing about its scale or influence: it is placed only so that its relations are easy to follow.

maps.name: 03 C1 Salt builds, and farms respond in steps
maps.description: *Root zone salinity* damages the *Soil structure*, so less rain soaks in to refill the lens: the *Rainwater lens thickness in the low polders* falls over years and *Root zone salinity* rises further (R1). As *Harvest lost to salt* rises, and after the dry summers that bring the damage to notice, farmers respond in different ways, and at different speeds: *Adoption of salt-tolerant varieties* of their current crops, with the same machines and storage (B1); *Adoption of new crops*, new to the island's rotations, which need a market and their own machines (B2); and, over decades, less *Arable land in the polders* where arable farming stops paying, which raises the *Water board's plans to raise ditch levels*, since its levels follow the land's use (B3). The first two lower the *Harvest lost to salt* and leave the salt in the soil; only the third lowers the salt. The order is a reading of the costs, since the first two wait alike for the damage to show, and of the decades B3 takes; and the links from *Harvest lost to salt* to *Adoption of salt-tolerant varieties* and from *Agricultural land value* to *Arable land in the polders* are hypotheses for the group model building session.

maps.name: 04 C2 Low ditch levels: workable fields now, more demand later
maps.description: A lower *Ditch level (NAP)* gives a greater *Polder drainage depth*, which raises the *Spring workability of the fields* within the season, so *Farmers' demand for deep polder drainage* eases (B4). The same lower level raises *Saline seepage (kwel)*, which over years lowers the *Rainwater lens thickness in the low polders*. *Root zone salinity* and *Harvest lost to salt* rise, *Farm income* and *Agricultural land value* fall. *Financial leverage*, *Banks' risk assessment of farm loans*, the *Risk premium on farm loans* and *Debt payments* rise, and thus the farm's *Dependence on high-margin salt-sensitive crops*, which in spring needs deep drainage, grows: the demand returns higher (R2). The relief comes first and the extra demand years later, also known as the “Fixes that fail” archetype (Kim, 2000, p. 16). The link from *Debt payments* to *Dependence on high-margin salt-sensitive crops* is a hypothesis for the group model building session.

maps.name: 05 C3 Debt and capital together keep a farm in its crops
maps.description: *Debt payments* raise the farm's *Dependence on high-margin salt-sensitive crops* (R2, a hypothesis), and so does the *Capital lost on switching to new crops* (R3, on sources). Each loop raises the variable that drives the other: more dependence brings more *Spending on keeping the current crops*, so more *Machines and storage for the current crops* and more capital a switch would write off (R3). This causes more *Farmers' demand for deep polder drainage* (R2). Dependence on current crops holds back the adaptation of new crops. Salt, on its own, lowers that dependence over the years as the current crops yield worse harvests due to increasing root-zone salinity.

maps.name: 06 C4 The quick answer to a dry summer goes first
maps.description: Three loops are connected to *Crop water shortfall*, which happen at different speeds: *Groundwater extraction for irrigation* within the season (B5); *Freshwater storage measures*, over the years the *Rainwater lens thickness in the low polders* takes to grow (B6); and a *Freshwater supply route to the island*, after the years it takes to decide, pay for and build a supply route, which the island does not have yet (B7; Tiekstra, 2023, Regenwater section). Whatever eases the shortfall first lowers the pressure for the slower answers. Extraction is tied to what it draws on (B8): *Pumping the water board allows* depends on the *Freshwater lens thickness under creek ridges and dunes*, since the water board's rules let farms pump for irrigation without a permit, up to 60 m³ an hour, 3,000 m³ a quarter and 8,000 m³ a year and notified at least four weeks ahead, where its map shows a fresh groundwater body outside its vulnerable areas, one at least 15 m thick or reaching the geohydrological base (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2026f, arts. 1.1 and 4.8 b and f).

maps.name: 07 C5 Storing: more worthwhile, harder to pay for
maps.description: *Freshwater storage measures* lower the *Winter rain drained away*, so more rain refills the lens and, over years, the *Rainwater lens thickness in the low polders* rises; *Freshwater availability for crops* rises, the *Crop water shortfall* falls and *Crop yield* rises. There the two loops part. A larger *Crop water shortfall* makes storing more worthwhile to a farmer (B6), and through a lower *Crop yield* leaves less *Farm income* and less *Farmers' capacity to invest* (R4), so the same dry year pushes storage up and down. Farms with the means store and farms without may not; which pull is stronger differs per farm. The link from *Farmers' capacity to invest* to *Freshwater storage measures* is a hypothesis for the group model building session.

maps.name: 08 C6 Salt losses raise the wish to switch and cut the means
maps.description: A higher *Harvest lost to salt* makes *Adoption of new crops* more worthwhile, after a delay (B2). The same losses lower *Farm income* and *Agricultural land value*, so *Financial leverage* and the *Banks' risk assessment of farm loans* rise, *Bank credit to farms* falls and the *Farmers' capacity to invest* in the switch falls (R6); less credit adds less to *Farm debt* and keeps leverage down (B9). A field that moves saves harvest from salt (R6) and raises the *Margin given up on high-margin crops* (B10). The level of salt in the soil of the farmland decides whether switching is economically beneficial or not.

maps.name: 09 C7 New crops stay stuck or take off
maps.description: With few hectares of *Adoption of new crops* there is little harvest for a plant to process, no *Local processing capacity for new crops*, and transport keeps the *Net price for new crops after transport* low (R7). Every field that starts being used for new crops raises the *Margin given up on high-margin crops*, which *Farm income* and *Bank credit to farms* must carry (B10): adoption stays low. With enough hectares a local plant becomes worthwhile, the net price rises and more farmers grow the crop. How many hectares that takes is unclear from the literature and thus not clear in the CLD.

maps.name: 10 C8 One ditch level between four goals
maps.description: Four balancing loops act on the *Water board's plans to raise ditch levels*, each towards its own goal. Fields dry enough for heavy machinery in spring (*Spring workability of the fields*, B4); the fresh water lenses the board wants to keep as a measure against *Saline seepage (kwel)* (B11); the optimum Polder drainage depth the board's norms aim at for each use and soil type (B12); and a plan the objecting owners can accept (*Objections to land-use plans*, B13). The goals cannot all be met at once, so the level settles where those pressures balance. How far seepage weighs against the other goals in the board's plans, cannot be determined from the literature found.

maps.name: 11 C9 Objections to one plan shape the next
maps.description: *Objections to land-use plans* delay, change or stop a plan (B13). Two things follow: The ditch levels keep up the *Saline seepage (kwel)* and *Root zone salinity* that lower *Agricultural land value*, and a lower value may bring more objections (R8). Plans changed or dropped lower *Farmers' trust in government*, which may bring more objections to the next plan (R9). Whether objections settle at a plan the owners accept or keep growing is a question for the group model building session: two of its links are hypotheses, from *Agricultural land value* to *Objections to land-use plans* and from *Objections to land-use plans* to *Farmers' trust in government*.

maps.name: 12 C10 Falling land value: levels held, or land leaving arable
maps.description: The three loops share the chain from the *Water board's plans to raise ditch levels* through *Ditch level (NAP)*, *Saline seepage (kwel)*, *Rainwater lens thickness in the low polders*, *Root zone salinity* and *Harvest lost to salt* to *Farm income* and *Agricultural land value*, and part ways there. As land loses value, *Financial leverage* and *Debt payments* lead farmers to ask for deep drainage (R2), and owners may object harder to raises (R8, a hypothesis): both keep the ditch levels low and the salt coming. Where arable farming stops paying, *Arable land in the polders* falls, the board has more reason to raise the levels, and the salt falls back (B3). The same fall in value sends the water board opposite signals; which is stronger decides whether the decline persists or stops.

maps.name: 13 R1 Salty soil takes in less rain
maps.description: Salt in the root zone puts sodium on the clay; once fresh water washes the salt out, the soil's structure collapses and recovers only over years. Less rain soaks in, less recharges the rainwater lens, the lens thins over years and saline groundwater comes closer to the roots: more salt. It runs in the low polders. The mechanism was measured after seawater floods; how much sodium the island's seepage puts on its clay, no source read shows. R1 may be weak on tile-drained fields such as the one measured on the island: in model computations extra winter water leaves through the intensive drainage without feeding the lens (de Louw et al., 2015, pp. 11, 12), and after a seawater flood most well-drained soils still let at least 150 mm through in winter (van Beekom et al., 1953a, p. 157). No practice is on it: the salt it adds drives tolerant crops and varieties (B2, B1).

maps.name: 14 B1 Salt losses move fields to tolerant varieties
maps.description: The more harvest salt takes, the more a tolerant variety is worth against the one grown now, so after the dry summers that bring the damage to notice, and perhaps only past a threshold, more farmers grow it. A tolerant variety loses less to salt, so the harvest lost falls. It seeks the loss at which a farmer changes variety, a hypothesis for the group model building session: unlike the move to new crops (B2), no source shows that salt losses move farmers to another variety. Tolerant varieties use the same machines, storage and know-how, so little capital is lost on them (R3). It drives tolerant varieties.

maps.name: 15 B2 Salt losses move fields to new crops
maps.description: The more harvest salt takes, the more a new crop that copes with salt is worth against the current crops, so after the dry summers that bring the damage to notice, and perhaps only past a threshold, more farmers grow it. A field moved no longer has a conventional harvest for salt to take, so the harvest lost falls; the salt stays in the soil. It seeks the loss at which a farmer switches: that farmers hold back until salt severely hits their production rests on sources, what sets each farmer's threshold, through their crops, margins, buyers and bank, is a hypothesis for the group model building session. On the island no source read shows B2 at work: the shift its farmers show is from onions to cereals, a crop they already grow and no new one, which the source puts down to drought (Raat et al., 2026, p. 49). With B1 and B3 it is a way out of the same salt: switching keeps the land arable, B3 is arable farming ending. It drives new crops.

maps.name: 16 B3 Land leaving arable use lets levels rise and salt fall
maps.description: More salt in the root zone takes more of the harvest, income and land value fall, and where arable farming no longer pays for a buyer or successor the land goes to a holder who does not farm it as arable land. With less arable land the water board, whose level follows the land's use, has more reason to raise the ditch levels, over years; seepage falls, the rainwater lens thickens and the salt falls back. It seeks the salt level at which arable farming stops paying for any successor or buyer, set by crop prices, margins and the land market. With B2 and B1 it is a way out of the same salt: those keep the land arable with another crop, this one is arable farming ending, where the current crops stop paying and adapting does not pay or is not chosen. It acts only at that end: while arable farming still pays for someone, land from a farm that stops mostly goes to expanding neighbours and stays arable (Arable land in the polders), and a raise follows only where a whole level area leaves arable use, since where nature and farmland share one on Duiveland the plan keeps nature's level and keeps the farm parcel draining (Arable land in the polders → Water board's plans to raise ditch levels). On Duiveland most raises wait for more discharge capacity, and the province's norm for storage and discharge holds for grassland as for arable land (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, pp. 12, 33–34, 69), so, by inference, a level area that goes from arable crops to grass would mostly still wait for the discharge works, and the loop is weaker still there. From salt to a raise takes decades, its slowest steps the land changing hands and the board's plan cycle.

maps.name: 17 B4 Deep drainage keeps fields workable
maps.description: Where fields stay too wet to work in spring, farmers ask for low ditch levels and the water board plans fewer raises. The levels stay low, the fields drain and dry sooner, and the wish for lower levels eases. On Duiveland it has room mainly in the 10 of 31 level areas with more than 10% of their surface too wet in a normal winter, since in large parts of the area the drooglegging already exceeds its optimum by more than 40 cm (60 cm on schorgronden) (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, pp. 32, 42). It seeks fields dry enough for heavy machinery in spring: what deep drainage gains a farm, R2 tracing what it costs. By keeping the current crops' spring work possible, it supports carrying on with them rather than adopting a practice.

maps.name: 18 R2 Debt and deep drainage feed each other through salt
maps.description: A farm with higher leverage is a riskier loan, so banks charge a higher premium and its debt payments rise. To meet them it keeps its high-margin, salt-sensitive crops, whose spring soil work needs fields that dry early, so farmers ask for low ditch levels and the water board, weighing that against raising them, plans fewer raises. The levels stay low, saline seepage stays higher, the rainwater lens thins over years, salt takes more of the harvest, income and land value fall, and leverage rises. It closes only through a hypothesis, Debt payments → Dependence on high-margin salt-sensitive crops, which no source read tests; where indebted farms choose less risky crops instead, the loop breaks there. It shows an unintended consequence of the deep drainage in B4: the gain comes within the season, the seepage and salt years later. It holds back new crops through the dependence it keeps up, while the salt it adds pushes towards them (B2, B1).

maps.name: 19 R3 Capital ties farms to their crops
maps.description: A farm tied to its current crops spends on keeping them as machines and stores fall due, over years. The more it owns for those crops, the more a switch to a new crop would write off, and what it would lose ties it further to them. It holds back new crops, and leaves tolerant varieties of the current crops nearly untouched. On Schouwen-Duiveland R3 may be weak: its farm-level evidence is a store built in the Limburg loess and one farmer's plans for water storage, while the island's own farmer ties the low cost of a less intensive rotation there to the lack of fresh water, and the workshop and an exploration of the island tie the share of sensitive crops to it and to drought (Dijkshoorn-Dekker et al., 2024, pp. 56–57, 59, 71; Raat et al., 2026, pp. 34, 49).

maps.name: 20 B5 Pumping relieves the shortfall
maps.description: As the crop water shortfall grows, farmers pump more fresh groundwater, crops get more water and the shortfall shrinks, within the season. It seeks the water the crop needs, and runs only where a farm has fresh groundwater more than 15 m thick under it, on the creek ridges and dunes; the farmers talked to in the low polders do not irrigate. Across the whole island it can move little: groundwater irrigation, taken at the permitted maximum, a figure the authors call probably inaccurate, is about one hundredth of the 2018 precipitation deficit (Krajenbrink et al., 2023, pp. 44–46, 48). Where it eases the shortfall it eases the worse harvests that make storing worthwhile (B6), so it can hold storage back.

maps.name: 21 B6 Farms store water when water falls short
maps.description: As the water falls short of what crops need, farmers find storing it more worthwhile and those who can pay for it store more. Less winter rain drains away, the rainwater lens thickens over years, crops on that field have more fresh water and the shortfall shrinks. It seeks the shortfall at which storing stops being worth its cost, which each farmer sets against their other ways through a dry summer. On the island's two trials of the lens-growing measures the lens's growth was not clearly shown: at Kerkwerve freshening was measured at 3 of 5 locations and the effect 'lijkt daarmee beperkt' (Oude Essink et al., 2018, p. 97), and near Dreischor its growth was '(nog) niet aangetoond' over the measuring period, perhaps because of height differences within the plot or because the fresh-salt system responds slowly (van Hateren et al., 2025, p. 59). It drives storage, slowly, the lens taking years to respond.

maps.name: 22 B7 A shortfall brings calls for a supply route
maps.description: The shorter of water the farms, the more firmly Agrarisch Schouwen-Duiveland asks for a supply route, and the deciding body weighs that call over the years a route takes to decide, pay for and build. A route would carry fresh water to the island, crops would have more to draw on and the shortfall would shrink. A route drawing on the Volkerak-Zoommeer would ease the shortfall little late in the season, when algae closed such inlets on Tholen in most years 2003–2011 (Schipper et al., 2014, p. 36); the Haringvliet source with a ring pipeline gives the best water but the highest costs (Witteveen+Bos, 2021, p. 50). None exists, so the loop has not run yet; a study has left open who pays and who would run one. It seeks a shortfall the deciding body finds acceptable. Where it eased the shortfall it would ease the worse harvests that make storing worthwhile (B6).

maps.name: 23 B8 Pumping rules protect the lens
maps.description: Under the creek ridges and dunes, the thicker the fresh groundwater, the more pumping the water board's rules allow. Farmers pump within that, and what they pump beyond what the rain puts back thins the lens. It seeks the balance between recharge and extraction on which the board set its limit. On the island the rules answer the lens at the 15 m threshold, not along it: a lens that thins while still at 15 m or more keeps the same 800 m³ per hectare (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2026f, arts. 1.1 and 2.9), and after a map revision leaves wells outside the fresh bodies, those in use may still be used and only new ones are refused (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2019, p. 20). It shows an unintended consequence of the pumping in B5: a thinner lens, which reaches crops only through wells, so it comes back only through what the rules allow. For storage on the creek ridges, what infiltration adds to this lens is what wells can pump.

maps.description: A farm with more left to invest can pay for more storage measures, so less winter rain drains away, more recharges the rainwater lens, the lens thickens over years, crops on that field have more fresh water, the shortfall shrinks, and yield, income and what the farm can invest rise. It runs in the low polders. It drives storage on farms with the means and holds it back on farms without.

maps.description: Lower ditch levels raise the saline seepage. The water board names the salinisation a concern and aims to keep or enlarge the lenses, so over years more seepage gives it more reason to plan raises; once carried out, the levels rise and the seepage falls. It seeks the fresh water in the soil the board wants to keep; how far seepage weighs against drought in its plans, no source read shows. On the island the board's accounts read give the loop little support: the board raises levels on Schouwen to limit drought damage, with larger fresh water stocks in the soil as the effect (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021b, p. 53), and its 2025 framework for level plans names neither seepage nor the lenses among its criteria (2025, pp. 9, 12), so of the accounts read only the Duiveland report names the lenses among its reasons for a raise (2021a, p. 37). It touches adoption only through the salt it lowers (B2, B1).

maps.name: 31 B12 The board tests the drainage depth
maps.description: The water board tests each level area's drainage depth against the optimum for its use and soil: where little of the area is too wet a raise is considered, where much of it is the target level is lowered or the discharge's bottlenecks solved. Carried out over years, the depth moves back towards that optimum, which the board sets by its own rules. It touches adoption only through the seepage and salt the ditch level sets.

maps.name: 32 B13 Objections hold back plans
maps.description: A plan to raise ditch levels brings objections, appeals and lobbying from landowning farmers who expect it to lower their land's value; whether that is their reason is a question for the group model building session. Objections can delay, change or stop the plan while it is pending, so fewer raises stay planned. On the island the views changed neither 2021 level plan, as the board summarises them, not Schouwen's raise in ten level areas nor Duiveland's proposed study of a raise (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021b, pp. 8, 53; 2021a, p. 53), so no source read shows objections holding back a raise there. It is the objectors' intended loop, protecting their land, and seeks a plan they can accept. It touches adoption only through the levels it holds, and through R8 and R9.

maps.name: 33 R8 Falling land value brings objections that keep salt high
maps.description: When farmland loses value, its owners may object harder to the next plan to raise ditch levels; whether they do is a hypothesis for the group model building session, the sign possibly opposite where compensation pays more than the land would fetch. Objections can hold today's level while a plan is pending, and never deepen it. Seepage stays higher, the rainwater lens stays thin, salt takes more of the harvest, income falls and the land loses more value. It shows an unintended consequence of the objections in B13: owners object to protect their land, and the levels held keep up the seepage and salt that lower its value. It touches adoption through the salt it keeps up (B2, B1).

maps.name: 34 R9 Changed plans erode trust
maps.description: Objections and appeals delay, change or stop plans after public bodies have announced them. Plans changed or dropped teach farmers not to count on the next one, their trust in government falls, and farmers who trust less object more. The step from objections to trust is a hypothesis for the group model building session; the step from trust back to objections rests on sources. It reinforces where farmers' objections are passed over, or through the conflict itself; where a body takes them up, the step may turn positive and the loop balancing. It holds back storage, a long investment that a change of rules can strand, as trust falls.

maps.name: 35 B15 The water sets the crops
maps.description: The more of the rotation is under the high-margin crops, the more water the crop plan needs and, with the water the island has, the larger the shortfall; over years, farms short of water move off those crops, sown onions first, and the shortfall shrinks. It seeks a crop plan the island's water can carry: the water is a limit farmers fit their crops to, as much as the salt. On the island the sown onions fell from 1,214 ha in 2015 to 791 ha in 2022 (Delphy, 2023, p. 15). It holds back the income the high-margin crops bring, so where a farm adapts this way it adapts by earning less.
